articles.title: US Reportedly Plans to ‘Offer’ Ukraine EU Membership for Dropping NATO Bid - Kyiv Post
articles.summary: US Reportedly Plans to ‘Offer’ Ukraine EU Membership for Dropping NATO Bid  Kyiv Post
articles.full_text:
A US peace proposal would ‘offer’ Ukraine European Union membership and an investment package in exchange for abandoning its bid to join NATO, The Economist reported on Thursday, Oct. 22.
The reported outline also includes a demilitarized zone in Donbas, the eastern Ukrainian region comprising Donetsk and Luhansk.
Russia could receive commercial agreements with American companies, sanctions relief and restored political ties with Washington. The package also envisages resuming Russian gas supplies to Europe, including reviving Nord Stream, according to the report.
Ukrainian officials are familiar with the general framework but have not received full details of the latest US proposals, The Economist reported. Neither Kyiv nor Washington has announced that Ukraine has accepted the terms.
One Ukrainian official told the magazine that Kyiv fears US representatives could pursue lucrative deals with Moscow before the war ends, allowing Russia to gain economic and diplomatic benefits while fighting continues.
Kyiv seeks enforceable security guarantees
The reported outline follows talks in Oslo on Oct. 20 between President Volodymyr Zelensky, US envoy Steve Witkoff and European leaders. The discussions covered Ukraine’s security, territorial questions, sanctions and postwar economic prospects.
US officials described work on two tracks: Ukraine’s sovereignty, security guarantees, European integration and reconstruction; and a separate framework addressing Russia and future security arrangements.
Witkoff subsequently met Russian President Vladimir Putin in St. Petersburg on Oct. 21.
After that meeting, Zelensky said Washington had relayed that Moscow was open to resuming trilateral negotiations with Ukraine and the US. He said the teams could meet by early November, although no date had been set.
The Kremlin then indicated that Putin was ready in principle to resume talks around mid-November.
Kyiv is pressing for security commitments it considers enforceable. Zelensky has said Ukraine is negotiating US guarantees modeled on NATO’s Article 5 and backed by a vote in Congress.
He described NATO membership, bilateral US guarantees and a European-led Coalition of the Willing as complementary parts of Ukraine’s security framework. No final agreement on those guarantees has been announced.
Washington cannot grant EU membership
The reported offer does not establish an agreed accession date or mean Ukraine would automatically join the EU.
Under the EU’s accession rules, membership requires negotiations, the European Parliament’s consent, unanimous approval by the Council and ratification of an accession treaty by all member states and the candidate country.
A previous US-backed peace framework reportedly proposed that Ukraine could join the EU as soon as January 2027. Kyiv Post reported in December 2025 that the proposal would involve territorial concessions and require Brussels to consider changes to its enlargement process. That was a proposed timetable, not an agreed accession date.
Renewed Russian energy supplies would also require European decisions. The EU adopted a legally binding phaseout of Russian gas imports in January, with remaining long-term LNG supplies due to end from January 2027 and pipeline supplies from autumn 2027.
As Kyiv Post previously reported, Germany’s government opposes reopening Nord Stream, which also faces US and EU sanctions.
The reported package therefore includes benefits Washington cannot deliver alone. Ukraine’s accession and any lasting return of Russian gas to the EU market would require agreement in Europe, alongside a settlement accepted by Kyiv and Moscow.

articles.full_text:
Home |News |Piyush Goyal Warns Europe On Cbam 50 Pc Steel Duty Says Trust Hardest Currency In Business
Piyush Goyal warns Europe on CBAM, 50 pc steel duty; says trust hardest currency in business
Piyush Goyal warned that Europe’s carbon border mechanism and high steel import duties could increase living costs and hurt industries. He projected India-Germany trade could reach €310 billion, while highlighting the proposed India-EU FTA and cooperation in strategic sectors
New Delhi: Commerce and Industry Minister Piyush Goyal has warned European countries that the Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM) and high import duties on steel could raise cost of living, make industries uncompetitive and hurt consumers.
During a question and answer session at the Berlin Global Dialogue 2026, the minister said, “If you have put a CBAM on yourself, you put a 50 per cent import duty to bring steel into your country, you are inviting disaster. He noted that trust is the hardest currency in commerce today. “Your cost of living will go up. Your people will be unhappy. Your industry will be out priced,” Goyal added.
Speaking at another programme in Berlin, the minister noted that India-Germany bilateral trade could rise to €310 billion from around €31 billion at present if the two countries focus on complementary strengths and jointly create products and technologies. However, he did not specify a timeline for achieving the target.
Notably, Goyal is on an official visit to Germany and the Netherlands from October 22 to 27 and was accompanied by a delegation of about 100 Indian businesses and startups. Meanwhile, German Federal Minister for Economic Affairs and Energy Katherina Reiche called for reducing red tape on both sides and undertaking joint projects, saying bilateral trade could be doubled.
Addressing the India-Germany Business Roundtable and inaugurating the India Centre of the German Council on Foreign Relations (DGAP), Goyal said the India-EU free trade agreement (FTA) is expected to be signed by the end of this year and could become operational within the next four to five months.
Apart from that, Goyal and Reiche held a bilateral meeting earlier in the day and discussed cooperation in artificial intelligence, semiconductors, energy and other sectors. “Discussed opportunities in AI, semiconductors, advanced manufacturing, critical minerals, green hydrogen, renewable energy, energy storage, and resilient supply chains, as well as increased investment in India’s industrial and digital ecosystems,” Goyal said in a social media post.
“We also exchanged views on how the India-EU FTA will prove to be a game-changer that would help businesses in both India and Germany realise their full potential,” he added.

articles.title: Europe’s Midterm Calculation: Why a Weakened Trump Means a Harder Line on NATO - Modern Diplomacy
articles.summary: Europe’s Midterm Calculation: Why a Weakened Trump Means a Harder Line on NATO  Modern Diplomacy
articles.full_text:
Four Options, Three Days Later
On 6 November, three days after Americans vote, Pentagon officials are due to put at least four courses of action for America’s military footprint in Europe in front of Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth. They are the product of a posture review that Elbridge Colby, the Pentagon’s policy chief, says is meant to move NATO “fast and irreversibly” toward Europe taking primary responsibility for its own conventional defence — and of a questionnaire asking allies whether they restricted US use of their bases and airspace during the Iran war. A Pentagon official has already spoken of “clearly at least some demand signal” for options that downgrade US forces. Many in European capitals read the timing as lucky: a president humbled at the ballot box, the reasoning goes, will be in no position to gut the alliance. That reading is backwards. A weakened Trump is likely to be a harder one on NATO.
A President Losing Altitude — and an Alliance Already Sorted
The numbers are bleak for the White House. A Reuters/Ipsos poll put Trump’s approval at 31% on 19 October, the lowest of his career, with Democrats 12 points ahead on the generic ballot. Decision Desk HQ’s model gives Democrats a 78% chance of taking the House and 57% of taking the Senate. The main drag is the US-Israeli war on Iran, launched on 28 February, which pushed diesel to a record $6.52 a gallon in September.
The war has also become the organising grievance of Trump’s NATO policy. When European allies declined to help secure the Strait of Hormuz in the spring, Trump openly mused about leaving the alliance. Since then the Pentagon has cancelled an armoured brigade rotation to Poland and announced up to 5,000 troop cuts, mainly in Germany, and convened a “Bergen Group” of favoured allies — Germany, Poland, the Netherlands, Norway, Sweden and Finland — that pointedly excludes Britain, France and the Baltic states. Congress has drawn lines of its own: a 2023 law bars withdrawal from NATO without Senate or congressional approval, and the 2026 defence bill forbids cutting US forces in Europe below 76,000 without first consulting allies.
Congress Guards the Floor, Not the Ceiling
The case for optimism is intuitive. A Democratic House would control spending, wield subpoena power and hold a veto over the annual defence bill, and Republican senators already restive over Iran would feel freer to break ranks. Some of that is true. But it confuses two different things Congress can protect.
What Congress can legislate is the floor of the alliance: formal membership, troop numbers, the rule that an American general commands NATO forces in Europe. What it cannot legislate is the ceiling — the credibility of the American promise to fight. Deterrence under Article 5, NATO’s mutual-defence clause, lives in the Kremlin’s assessment of the president, not of the appropriations committee. A Trump who keeps 76,001 troops in Europe while telling a campaign rally, as he did on 20 October, that “we will have no choice but to leave” if allies do not “find their way” has complied with every statute while hollowing out the thing the statutes exist to protect.
More important is the direction in which domestic pressure has already pushed him. The clearest test came on 9 October. Facing record fuel prices four weeks before the vote, Trump struck a deal with Vladimir Putin for millions of tonnes of Russian diesel; the Treasury exempted cargoes from sanctions until April 2027 — the longest diesel waiver since 2022, and one that cut against a Russia sanctions law Trump had signed a month earlier. Electoral weakness did not make him more deferential to allies or to Congress. It made him willing to hand Moscow a concession, over Ukrainian and European objections, to move a domestic number.
The Bergen Group follows the same logic. Allies are now sorted by loyalty as much as by capability. The Pentagon’s questionnaire asks whether governments publicly back US foreign policy, and Politico reported that the administration had weighed a “naughty and nice list”. Analysts quoted by Euronews link Britain and France’s exclusion to their initial refusal to join the Iran war, and the Baltics’ to their rejection of Colby’s advice to soften their tone towards Moscow. This is not an incoherent policy waiting to be corrected. It is a coherent one — NATO as a tiered clientele — and it needs no congressional consent to function.
Trump’s own record points the same way. Six weeks after losing the House in 2018, he announced a withdrawal from Syria over his defence secretary’s objections; Jim Mattis resigned the next day. The New York Times later reported that Trump had repeatedly told aides that year he wanted to leave NATO. Presidents who lose leverage at home turn to the arena where they act alone. Trump, whose foreign policy already runs on executive orders, sanctions licences and phone calls, has less to lose from a hostile Congress than any modern predecessor. As a recent Modern Diplomacy analysis put it, a defeated president becomes hurried rather than cautious.
The strongest objection is that the Republican coalition is already cracking on precisely these issues. Mitch McConnell publicly rebuked Trump’s NATO threats in April; four Republican senators voted in September to end the Iran war; farm-state Republicans forced a reversal on diesel exports. A bad night on 3 November would speed this up, and a party turning towards 2028 may want distance from an unpopular president’s feuds with allies.
The dynamic is real, but it buys less than it appears. Several of the loudest dissenters, McConnell and Thom Tillis among them, are retiring. The September war-powers resolution still failed 50–49 — the twentieth attempt. Overriding a veto takes two-thirds of both chambers, a margin no forecast offers. Defections limit what Trump can get Congress to do; they barely touch what he can do without it.
So Europe does gain room — in Washington’s legislature rather than its executive, and only briefly. The 2027 defence bill passed the House 216–212 in July but stalled in the Senate, so it will almost certainly be finished in the “lame-duck” session between the election and January. The House version would extend the 76,000-troop floor, order a review of whether the 5,000-troop cut broke last year’s law, and force the Pentagon to justify its posture decisions. That is where European diplomatic energy belongs this winter.
Three Ways the Winter Could Go
Base case — the same policy, delivered harder (55%). Democrats take the House and possibly the Senate. Trump reads the result as proof of disloyalty from allies who “weren’t there”, not as a mandate for moderation. The posture review produces cuts that keep US forces just above the 76,000 floor; Bergen-style sorting widens, with Denmark — fresh from a Greenland basing deal — reportedly next in line; Russia policy keeps bending to fuel prices. There is no formal exit, only steady erosion of credibility. The key assumption: Trump stays inside the legal guardrails while probing their edges.
Downside — the guardrails get tested (25%). The Iran war widens — Washington has already ordered most embassy staff out of Saudi Arabia amid Houthi attacks — and the Pentagon cites operational necessity to pull air defences, munitions and support units out of Europe faster than the consultation rules allow, daring a new Democratic House to litigate. The damage is less numerical than political: Europe learns that the floor itself is negotiable. For governments and companies exposed to NATO’s eastern flank, this is the scenario least priced in.
Upside — Congress locks the floor in place (20%). A chastened Republican Senate leadership and a Democratic House use the lame-duck defence bill to entrench Europe’s posture; Hegseth picks the mildest of his four options; Trump’s attention moves to an Iran settlement and the December G20 summit in Miami, to which he has invited Putin. Europe gets a calmer 2027 — but on borrowed time, because the shift towards Colby’s “NATO 3.0” continues regardless.
Prepare for the Same Policy, Only Harder
Europe’s midterm calculation should not turn on whether Trump will be weaker after 3 November. He almost certainly will be. The question is where that weakness shows. It will show in Congress. It will not show in the policy that matters most to Europe, which runs through the Oval Office, the Pentagon’s posture review and the president’s phone line to Moscow. Governments that spend the winter waiting for a chastened president will be surprised; those that spend it working the lame-duck Congress and speeding up their own rearmament will not.
The signal to watch is the final text of the 2027 defence bill in December: does it extend the 76,000-troop floor and attach conditions to whichever option Hegseth picks? If it does, Europe has bought time. If it does not, the floor was always a courtesy. Either way, NATO’s next chapter will be written by a president with less to lose than ever.

articles.title: France and Germany offer to supply Argentina submarines amid Falklands threat as No10 seeks EU reset - GB News

France and Germany's top defence firms are offering Argentina a fearsome new submarine fleet as Andy Burnham seeks closer ties with the European Union.
Downing Street has been warned a lethal upgrade to President Javier Milei's navy could be a “game changer” for Britain's ability to protect the Falkland Islands from future Argentinian aggression.
The damning revelation comes after the Prime Minister pledged to “bring the UK closer to Europe” following a meeting with German Chancellor Friedrich Merz earlier this month.
The Labour leader visited Berlin to ratify the 2025 Kensington Treaty — a sweeping security pact designed to deepen both nations’ relationship against hostile powers.
During the trip to the German capital, Mr Burnham confirmed he was open to Germany joining the Global Combat Air Programme (GCAP) — an initiative between Britain, Italy and Japan to develop a cutting-edge new fighter jet.
Mr Burnham also told the Commons last week it would be a “dereliction of duty” to turn down a closer relationship with Brussels ahead of a summit with the bloc next month.
Meanwhile, Argentina continues an aggressive posture toward the Falklands, with Mr Milei warning the United Nations General Assembly in New York his nation could be forced to “take matters into our own hands”.
As he demanded control of the British territory, the Argentine leader stressed he did not “believe in military solutions” to serve his country’s “national cause”.
Nevertheless, Mr Milei has overseen significant military expansion since coming to power, including the recent delivery of 12 F-16 Fighting Falcon fighter jets from Denmark, with another 12 planes set to be shipped in 2028.
Earlier this month, Argentina’s top military chief said Buenos Aires was seeking to acquire three new hunter-killer submarines for its navy.
Admiral Marcelo Dalle Nogare, Chief of the Joint Staff of Argentina’s Armed Forces, revealed Germany and France had both stepped forward to provide the boats.
“Whichever of the two options we choose, they are among the best submarines in the world today,” he told the Rotary Club of Buenos Aires on October 7.

The competing bids are from France’s Naval Group, which has proposed its Scorpène submarines, and Germany’s ThyssenKrupp Marine Systems (TKMS), which is offering its Type 209NG design.
According to Admiral Dalle Nogare, Paris and Berlin had offered to finance the submarine deal in full, with Buenos Aires repaying in instalments.
Neither government has publicly confirmed the reported financing arrangements. GB News can confirm TKMS has submitted an offer to Buenos Aires “based on the Argentine Navy’s requirements”.
The Kiel-based company told the People’s Channel it had not yet received any official communication from the Argentinian government, but added: “A decision in principle regarding the implementation of the programme is expected to be made in 2026."
Argentina has a history of operating German-built Type 209 submarines, including the ARA Salta and ARA San Luis, acquired in the 1970s.
During the 1982 Falklands War, San Luis patrolled and launched torpedo attacks against British warships but scored no hits. Despite technical faults, it evaded British anti-submarine forces and remained in service until 1997.
Admiral Dalle Nogare informed the Rotary Club the “final decision will ultimately be a geopolitical one, based on interests and, above all, financing” and expected the boats to be delivered six years after the contract is signed.
The French state currently holds a controlling majority stake in Naval Group, owning 62.25 per cent of the company's shares at the end of 2024.
Although Germany's government does not own TKMS, it retains a central role in deciding whether to export German-made military equipment.
As such, a deal to supply Argentina with three advanced submarines would require authorisation from the relevant government.
While discussing the proposed submarine acquisition, Admiral Dalle Nogare made an ominous prediction about the Falkland Islands, according to Argentinian publication El Cronista.
“I’ve always said that I believe the Falklands will eventually be recovered on the day it is no longer economically feasible for the United Kingdom to maintain them,” he claimed.
The potential deal to bolster Argentina’s fleet with three advanced European submarines sparked major concern and calls for the UK Government to act.

“The Government should summon the ambassadors of France and Germany, and demand a full account of their actions,” demanded Mr Rossindell, who previously served on the Nato parliamentary assembly UK delegation.
Mr Rossindell lodged a written question to the Ministry of Defence on the topic. The backbencher received what he described as a “non-answer” and “politicking” from ministers.
“The Ministry of Defence is committed to maintaining a defensive military presence in the South Atlantic to ensure the protection of the Falkland Islands,” she added.
Robert Midgley, a spokesman for the Friends of the British Overseas Territories, fumed: “The potential rearming of Argentina by Nato allies is a diplomatic failure of the British state.
“The UK Government has allowed the threat to the Falkland Islands to grow. For the past year, diplomatic staff across South America have sounded the alarm over Argentine lobbying efforts to gain allies to rally against the Falkland Islands.
“As ever, self-determination comes first, and the population of the Falklands have repeatedly voted against any transfer of sovereignty, which should be respected.”

“We're so reliant on other nations getting involved (in our defence), including the Germans, that we can't afford to pull the plug (on a potential deal)," he argued.
“Culturally and historically for the UK, French naval sales to Argentina carry heavy resonance,” former naval officer Stuart Fawcett commented.
“Most notably, the Exocet missile strikes that sank HMS Sheffield and SS Atlantic Conveyor, contributing to 46 British deaths (in 1982).
“That history looms large in public memory as we attempt to build a modernised bilateral relationship."
“The current defences of the Falkland Islands are much more advanced than the current Argentine threat and capable of repelling it, but if Argentina continues to re-arm and develop, then it may outpace and have the ability to overwhelm the current British forces on the Falklands,” he said.
A robust British defence force is currently stationed on the Falklands, including a squadron of Typhoon combat jets, refuelling tankers and cargo aircraft.

“We are in a position where, with the benefit of some of the other overseas territories in the South Atlantic, not least Ascension Island, we would be able to reinforce through there if we had to, in much the same way Ascension was used in 1982,” they said.
However, defence experts have warned these defences are primarily focused on countering air and surface threats.
They argued three high-tech European-made Argentinian submarines could fundamentally alter Britain’s approach to protecting the Falklands.
“If the angle was right and it positioned itself correctly, we wouldn't know about it until it hit something of ours... The first we'd know of it is a torpedo heading for the Queen Elizabeth,” he speculated, referencing one of the Royal Navy’s two flagship aircraft carriers.

articles.title: Could France's bond turmoil force the ECB's hand? - Euronews
articles.summary: Could France's bond turmoil force the ECB's hand?  Euronews
articles.full_text:
The European Central Bank is expected to hold rates next week as France's bond sell-off tightens borrowing conditions across the eurozone, while ECB President Christine Lagarde has made clear that the first steps to tackle French debt woes must come from Paris, not Frankfurt.
When the European Central Bank (ECB) meets next Thursday, it is widely expected to leave interest rates unchanged, partly because rising government bond yields are already pushing up borrowing costs across the eurozone.
ECB President Christine Lagarde has played down hopes of a rescue, saying the solution to France's debt problems lies at home.
The yield on France's 10-year government bond traded above 5% on Friday after rising to that level on Wednesday for the first time since 2002. The gap with German 10-year bonds, the eurozone's safest debt, was above 170 basis points.
Meanwhile, the 30-year yield was at 5.5%, and the gap with German 30-year bonds was even wider at 184 basis points.
On Thursday, the cost of France's five-year credit default swaps, contracts that insure investors against a government default, also climbed above 100 basis points for the first time since October 2012, when the eurozone was going through its sovereign debt crisis.
Lawmakers remain split over next year's budget, which includes €43 billion in spending cuts and additional revenue measures that the government has no majority to push through.
Ratings agency Moody's, which rates France Aa3, its fourth-highest grade, with a negative outlook, delivers its verdict on Friday evening, and a downgrade is widely expected. A one-notch cut to A1 would put France's rating at the equivalent level to those assigned by S&P and Fitch.
Civil unrest is adding to investors' concerns.
More protests are expected this weekend, and Paris police prefect Patrice Faure has advised business owners in a letter to hire private security.
French trade unions, unanimously disappointed after meeting Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu on Wednesday, have called for a large mobilisation on 5 November.
Sophie Binet, head of the CGT, one of France's biggest unions, urged workers to "generalise the strike".
Bonds doing the ECB's job
The case for another rate hike is still there.
The ECB has raised rates twice this year, lifting its deposit rate to 2.5%, and eurozone inflation jumped to 3.8% in September, driven by energy prices.
Yet German yields have climbed so much since September that their effect on growth and inflation roughly matches a 25 basis point hike, Carsten Brzeski, global head of macro at Dutch bank ING, estimated in an investor note on Thursday.
"For France, it’s closer to a 50 basis point hike," Brzeski wrote, adding that "the bond market has taken over the ECB's job".
Brzeski expects the ECB to wait for new staff forecasts in December before deciding on its next hike.
ECB President Christine Lagarde told the European Parliament on 28 September that long-term rates "have risen notably, which will slow growth".
Could the ECB intervene?
ECB officials have played down the possibility of intervening to lower France's borrowing costs, but have stopped short of ruling it out.
The central bank bought government bonds during the eurozone debt crisis to stabilise markets and ensure its rate decisions continued to feed through to the economy.
Speaking on the sidelines of the annual meetings of the International Monetary Fund and World Bank in Bangkok last week, Lagarde said that "there are particular circumstances that lead to some countries being more affected, France being a case in point."
"The primary and first solution lies at home in France. And it has to do with fiscal policies," the ECB president added.
Banque de France governor Emmanuel Moulin went further last Friday, saying the conditions for ECB intervention were not met at that time because there was no financial fragmentation in the eurozone.
However, both officials spoke before France’s 10-year borrowing costs rose above 5%.
If the ECB decides to intervene in the French bond market, one option could be the Transmission Protection Instrument (TPI), which was created in 2022 and has never been used.
The TPI lets the ECB buy the debt of countries whose borrowing costs climb in ways it judges unjustified by their economic fundamentals and threaten the transmission of monetary policy across the eurozone.
For a country to be eligible, it needs to meet several criteria, including following EU fiscal rules and keeping its debt on a sustainable path.
France is nursing a debt-to-GDP ratio of 119.1%, and the current budget negotiations offer little prospect of a quick reduction in the deficit, which is necessary to put the debt on a sustainable path.
Meanwhile, the government expects its debt-servicing costs to rise by more than €10 billion in 2027 compared with this year.
"The bar for activating the ECB's bond-buying programme remains high," Brzeski wrote in a separate investor note last week.
He added that, for France, that would at least mean passing its full budget. Acting too early could be "interpreted as monetary financing of the debt of a country unwilling to follow the rules," he warned.
The ECB's other emergency tool, Outright Monetary Transactions (OMT), was created in 2012 at the height of the eurozone debt crisis to allow unlimited purchases of a struggling country's short-term bonds.
However, it is only available to governments that first sign up to a bailout programme from the eurozone's rescue fund, the European Stability Mechanism.
Instead, Brzeski expects the ECB to quietly pause the reduction of its bond holdings, reinvesting maturing debt flexibly as it did during the COVID-19 pandemic.
Should turmoil spread to other eurozone bond markets, Brzeski sees TPI as a last resort. If France continued to fall short of EU fiscal rules, "the ECB might even consider purchasing bonds from almost all eurozone countries, except for France," he said.
For now, Brzeski sees next week’s rate meeting as "uneventful on action but clearly not on words".

articles.title: Burnham warned ‘Britain is at risk’ as a damning NATO ranking exposes UK’s military readiness crisis - London Business News
articles.summary: Burnham warned ‘Britain is at risk’ as a damning NATO ranking exposes UK’s military readiness crisis  London Business News
articles.full_text:
Defence Committee warns military readiness must improve before 2030, as Kemi Badenoch accuses the government of delaying crucial spending decisions and leaving Britain exposed to growing security risks.
Britain has been ranked second from bottom among NATO allies on an internal measure of how effectively members are meeting their rearmament commitments, raising fresh questions about the country’s ability to prepare for a potential Russian attack on the alliance before the end of the decade.
A report by the House of Commons Defence Committee places the UK 31st out of 32 NATO countries, with only Iceland — which has no military capability — ranked lower. The findings expose a gap between the government’s defence ambitions and the readiness of the armed forces, despite plans to invest almost £300bn over the next four years.
With British intelligence and other NATO assessments indicating that Russia could attack the alliance as soon as 2030, the committee warned that the timetable for addressing military weaknesses was becoming increasingly urgent.
“And if the UK government means what it says – that Russia could attack NATO as soon as 2030 – then work to rectify these vulnerabilities cannot start soon enough,” said Tan Dhesi, the Labour MP for Slough and chair of the committee.

The report described Britain’s position as stark. “According to an internal document apparently drawn up by NATO to measure how effectively members are meeting their rearmament promises, the UK is number 31 out of 32 Alliance countries,” it said.
The ranking intensifies scrutiny of whether the government’s planned spending increases will translate into forces capable of responding quickly to a crisis. Defence investment can fund new equipment, but deterrence also depends on existing ships, aircraft and other military assets being available, maintained and ready for deployment.
Ed Arnold, senior research fellow for European security at the Royal United Services Institute, told the committee that Britain’s position was “pretty poor”.
“The only way that you can increase that really is through cash because it’s all about fleet availability, it’s all about readiness to be out of the door as soon as possible and as soon as needed,” he said.
The government’s Defence Investment Plan, published in June, commits £298bn over the four years to 2029-30, with the aim of raising defence spending to 2.7 per cent of national income. A longer-term NATO commitment envisages Britain and its allies spending 3.5 per cent of national income on defence by 2035.
But the gap between those targets has become a source of political friction, with the Conservatives accusing ministers of postponing difficult decisions while warning that the security environment is deteriorating.
Kemi Badenoch, the Conservative leader, has called on the government to find additional money for defence in next week’s Budget, arguing that the necessary funding should be prioritised through welfare cuts and tighter control of borrowing.
“If, at this Budget, he does not find the money to get to 3%, John Healey has an awful lot of explaining to do,” she said in a speech in Westminster.
Badenoch described the delay in setting out a clear path towards higher defence spending as “unconscionable”, criticising reports that the decision had been deferred to a spending review that itself had been pushed back until next autumn.
She argued that the additional funding required to reach 3 per cent of gross domestic product by 2030 was “less than a third of the increase in welfare since Labour came to office”, framing the dispute as a question of government priorities rather than affordability alone.
“Britain is at risk,” she said. “John Healey said so himself, and no amount of political difficulty should prevent us from responding to that risk.”
Healey has argued that Britain must commit to spending 3 per cent of GDP on defence by 2030. The government is not expected to set out a full route towards NATO’s longer-term 3.5 per cent target until next year’s spending review, leaving uncertainty over the scale and timing of future funding.
The debate is particularly pressing for the Royal Navy, whose ability to operate in the High North is central to plans to deter Russian threats across the North Atlantic and surrounding waters.
The government is investing in its Hybrid Navy and Atlantic Bastion concepts, but the Defence Committee warned that the service’s current equipment readiness and platform numbers were substantially below its stated requirements.
“Royal Navy equipment readiness and platform numbers in particular are currently far worse than the government’s stated requirements,” the report said.
With 2030 identified as a key date for Britain to be ready to deter or defeat a Russian threat, the committee called for “dramatic progress” before the end of the decade to improve the availability and capabilities of the armed forces in the High North.
The Ministry of Defence told the inquiry that equipment was maintained at different levels of readiness according to operational requirements. Military platforms move through cycles of deployment, maintenance, training and preparation, with their readiness determined in part by the NATO capabilities they are expected to provide.
That distinction matters. A spending commitment is not the same as an operational capability, and a new platform offers limited immediate reassurance if existing equipment cannot be deployed when required.
The committee concluded that the near-£300bn investment programme was the bedrock of Britain’s contribution to deterring or defeating Russian aggression from 2030. But it also made clear that new procurement alone would not be enough: ministers must improve the readiness of the forces already in service.
The government now faces a difficult choice over how quickly to increase defence spending while balancing public services, welfare commitments and the cost of servicing national debt. The Conservatives are pressing for a faster commitment, while ministers must determine how to finance higher spending and convert it into military capability.
For Britain, the central question is whether its armed forces can become sufficiently equipped and ready before the strategic deadline identified by its own government. With the country near the bottom of NATO’s internal rearmament table, the committee’s warning is that the time available to close the gap is running short.

articles.full_text:
This week has seen EU negotiators hail growing “momentum” in UK ‘reset’ talks, as China fires warning over rumoured Electric Vehicle (EV) alignment.
With the Autumn Budget less than one week away, the Treasury has issued plans designed to cheer the UK business community, including extending import tariff suspensions on over 250 goods.
It was also a time for celebration, as the Chartered Institute celebrated trade professionals completing its qualifications at the 2026 graduation and prize-giving ceremony.
The big picture: There’s been continued progress towards the UK-EU reset outcomes proposed for this November’s bilateral summit, but talk of aligning on Chinese EV tariffs has prompted threats from Beijing.
This week, diplomats involved in negotiations told reporters there was “good momentum” towards the reset, with the three key asks from last year’s leaders’ summit “mostly agreed”.
However, ongoing pressure from Brussels for alignment on tariffs for imports of highly subsidised Chinese EVs has prompted threats of retaliatory trade measures from China.
A Chinese Ministry of Commerce spokesperson said that Beijing would “resolutely retaliate” in the event that the UK decided to adopt similar duties.
Brussels imposed substantial tariff rates on several Chinese car manufacturers after an anti-subsidy investigation in 2024, with companies such as BYD and Geely now facing total EU import tariffs of 27% and 28.8%, respectively.
Good week/bad week: A fantastic week for the UK’s trade sector, as we celebrated the 2026 Chartered Institute of Export & International Trade graduation and prize-giving ceremony.
Held in the heart of the capital at IET London: Savoy Place, we welcomed graduates from our own qualifications, the UK Customs Academy and IOEx Ltd apprenticeships to celebrate their professional achievements.
A UN body has found that an 18% cut back in global emissions is required within the next four years, to ensure we can “find our way back” on climate change.
That’s according to alarming findings shared by the UN Environment Programme (Unep).
The body warns that countries are failing to translate long-term emissions targets into short-term action.
The warning comes as the UK government made the decision to allow further extraction from the controversial Jackdaw gas field site in the North Sea.
How’s stat? £949.4bn. That was the value of UK exports in the 12 months to August 2026, according to the Department for Business, Innovation, Science and Trade’s updated quarterly trade figures.
This was an increase of 5.4% on the same figure from August 2025. Services exports were up 6.6%, while goods exports also increased by 4%.
In 2025, 41.3% of the UK’s exports (both goods and services) went to the EU, meaning the bloc remains the UK’s biggest export market. This was followed by the US, which received 21.8% of UK exports.
The changes refer to the value of the goods and services exported, not the volume.
Quote of the week: "While these extensions are welcome, we believe that government should be looking at the tariff suspension regime as a whole. This includes amending the ‘most favoured nation’ duty rate to 0% on goods where suspensions are continuously extended, and therefore reducing administrative burdens."
That was our technical director Anna Doherty FCIEx responding to the news that the government is set to extend tariff import suspensions on over 250 goods that were due to expire on 31 December.
The government estimates this will save businesses imports costs of £155m per year across sectors, such as "chemicals, plastics, hydrogen, automotive, and food and drinks industries".
Chancellor John Healey expanded on comments made earlier in the week that the upcoming Autumn Budget would be for “bloody-minded entrepreneurs and wealth creators”, as the government published a statement today (23 October) setting out those tariff plans, plus measures to reduce administrative burdens, in a bid to make doing business easier.
While welcoming the tariff announcement, Doherty set out how the government could go further. You can read her comments in full here.
You can also find out how those policies stack up against what Chartered Institute members said they wanted to see in the Budget.
What else we covered: Members can enjoy an update on news from the world of shipping in our latest ‘State of Freight’ feature, including predictions that the Strait of Hormuz may become “redundant” in the coming years. That comes as new trade routes are sought amid ongoing disruption in the Middle East.
For traders grappling with challenges stemming from Middle East disruption, as well as wider geopolitical uncertainty and ongoing regulatory change, there was also a write-up of our latest Global Trade Live webinar. That webinar, delivered in partnership with NatWest, addressed how the UK can build supply chain resilience in the face of such challenges.
True facts: Ukraine is pushing to shift customs checks on its agricultural exports to within the EU.
The proposal comes in response to increased Russian attacks on lorries queued at the border awaiting goods’ inspections.
Ukraine’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs spokesperson Heorhii Tykhyi characterised the situation as a “new security environment where Russia is deliberately trying to strike our borders, disrupt logistics, transportation, disrupt the cargo movement across the border”.
According to FT reporting, Kyiv is in talks with Poland and Slovakia about moving checks within their borders to make crossings safer for hauliers.

France has ordered four additional SAMP/T NG firing units, taking its total order for the ground-based air and missile defence system to twelve, according to eurosam.
The Organisation for Joint Armament Cooperation, known as OCCAR, placed the contract on behalf of France with eurosam, the Franco-Italian grouping formed by MBDA France, MBDA Italy and Thales. The units will be delivered to the French Air and Space Force in a multi-layer configuration combining Aster and MICA VL missiles.
The company said: “This order is an additional step towards the renewal of the European Long-Range Air and Missile Defence ground capabilities, following the SAMP/T NG development launched in 2021.”
It added: “OCCAR-EA, eurosam and its members, MBDA and Thales will continue to lead the way in state of the art and sovereign air and Missile defence systems for the benefit of European defence. These advanced air defence systems are crucial in the current global context to respond to increasingly challenging threats.”
A SAMP/T NG firing unit holds up to forty-eight Aster missiles ready to fire, carried across up to six launcher modules of eight rounds each, alongside a multi-function radar and identification module able to detect and identify targets beyond 350km, and an engagement module. The whole system is mobile and eurosam says it can be operational in under thirty minutes, offering 360-degree coverage and engaging targets beyond 150km.
The system is designed around the Aster 30 B1 and the newer Aster B1NT. The B1NT uses a Ka-band seeker and new interception algorithms to give what the company describes as a hit-to-kill capability against short and medium range ballistic missiles, low manoeuvring targets and hypersonic missiles.
Britain has a stake in the wider programme, since the United Kingdom is a participant in the FSAF-PAAMS arrangement that OCCAR manages, and the fourteenth amendment to that contract, signed in Paris in January 2024, covered supplementary procurement of equipment allowing Britain to carry out mid-life upgrades to its own Aster missiles. Aster is the weapon carried by the Royal Navy’s Type 45 destroyers as part of the Sea Viper system, which HMS Diamond used against Houthi missiles and drones in the Red Sea.
France and Italy have supplied SAMP/T systems to Ukraine, where the type has engaged Russian ballistic missiles.
The order lands while Britain has no ground-based long-range air defence system assigned to the defence of the United Kingdom. Luke Pollard, the Minister of State for Defence, confirmed this week that a further £790 million will be invested in homeland integrated air and missile defence, covering enhanced command and control, improved sensing and radar systems, counter-drone capabilities and more effective layered defences.
The Defence Committee reported yesterday that anti-strike capabilities for shooting down ballistic, hypersonic and cruise missiles and drones are among the capabilities European NATO members lack in sufficient numbers, and that replacing American military capabilities with European weapons has been costed by the Kiel Institute at an extra €50 billion each year over the next decade.

Realistically, though, our best path forwards for a true BMD shield is distributed naval launchers controlled by a mesh of land-based early warning radar, and medium-sized terminal defence guidance platforms.
Don’t disagree with having naval launchers however land based mobile launchers seem to me to be a simpler solution for most scenarios.

You might be thinking of the workup of HMS Dragon but being hard pressed to deploy a specialised warship to a specific area isn’t the same as not having any at all.
I also don’t want to overstate things as if the UK is flush with surface combatants at the moment by any means, but this statement was a bit farfetched.

A single SAMP/T unit usually has 6 trucks carrying 8 missiles, giving a battery 48 ready missiles. With 12 units, that could be 576 missiles ready to go.

articles.full_text:
The commerce minister warned that Europe's carbon levy and steel import restrictions could hurt manufacturers by making essential industrial inputs more expensive
Commerce and industry minister Piyush Goyal has criticized the European Union’s carbon border tax and steel import restrictions, warning that the measures could make European manufacturers less competitive and raise costs for consumers.
Speaking at the Berlin Global Dialogue on Thursday, 22 October, Goyal said Europe’s efforts to protect domestic industries risked making essential industrial inputs more expensive.
“Europe is shooting themselves in their own feet,” he said, referring to restrictions on steel imports, the Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM) and deforestation regulations.
Goyal questioned the logic of raising the cost of imported materials when European manufacturers need competitively priced steel, aluminum and other inputs.
“I would love to have high-tech products from Europe, your electrolyser coming to help me make green hydrogen, help me make green steel at much better prices,” he said.
“But you put a CBAM on yourself, you put a 50% duty to bring steel into your country, you are inviting disaster.”
His remarks came during an official visit to Germany and the Netherlands from 22 to 27 October, accompanied by a delegation of Indian businesses and startups.
Why India opposes the carbon levy
CBAM is designed to impose a carbon cost on certain imports comparable to the cost faced by manufacturers operating under the EU Emissions Trading System. The mechanism covers six sectors: iron and steel, aluminum, cement, fertilizers, electricity and hydrogen.
Its definitive phase began on 1 January 2026 following a transitional reporting period that started in October 2023. Financial obligations are being phased in as the EU gradually withdraws free carbon allowances for domestic producers.
Brussels argues that the mechanism prevents carbon leakage, where companies shift emissions-intensive production to countries with weaker climate regulations.
The European Commission has maintained that the system treats imported and domestically produced goods on comparable terms and encourages manufacturers outside the EU to reduce emissions.
India sees the policy differently.
Indian steel and aluminum producers rely heavily on carbon-intensive energy, leaving them exposed to additional costs when exporting to Europe. Companies must also meet emissions reporting and verification requirements.
The burden is particularly significant for steel. India’s average emissions intensity in steel production has been estimated at 2.54 tonnes of carbon dioxide per tonne of steel, compared with a global average of about 1.9 tonnes.
Higher emissions can translate into greater CBAM liabilities, although the actual amount depends on verified production emissions, applicable EU rules and carbon prices already paid in the country of origin.
New Delhi has also argued that climate-related trade measures should recognize differences in countries’ development levels and historical responsibilities for emissions.
That argument draws on the principle of common but differentiated responsibilities, under which developing economies should not be expected to bear identical obligations to wealthier industrialized countries.
Steel restrictions add to concerns
The EU introduced a revised tariff-rate quota system in July 2026, limiting the volume of certain steel products eligible for duty-free access. Imports exceeding applicable quotas face a 50% tariff.
The two measures operate differently. CBAM addresses embedded carbon emissions, while the steel quota system restricts imports to protect European producers. For manufacturers dependent on imported steel, however, the combined effect could be higher sourcing costs and fewer competitively priced alternatives.
European steelmakers have argued that stronger trade protections are necessary to counter global overcapacity and competition from lower-cost producers. Goyal’s position is that protecting upstream industries through trade barriers could impose costs on downstream manufacturers, including machinery, automotive and engineering businesses.
The disagreement comes as India and the EU move toward implementing their free trade agreement.
Goyal indicated that the agreement could be signed before the end of 2026 and become operational in early 2027, subject to the necessary approval procedures.
The agreement is expected to expand market access and reduce tariffs across a range of products, but it does not automatically eliminate obligations under CBAM.
India and the EU have discussed cooperation on carbon pricing, emissions measurement and industrial decarbonization. The European Commission has previously acknowledged the compliance challenges faced by Indian businesses and committed to continued technical engagement.

The market had expected a modest decline to 52.7, but the reading fell short of that. A reading above 50 indicates expansion, but the pace of growth is clearly slowing.
The main driver of the decline was the slump in France. Demand for goods and services there shrank amid heightened political uncertainty and fiscal pressure, pushing the PMI down to a level indicating contraction in activity. Business sentiment is at its lowest since 2012, excluding the COVID-19 pandemic period. In Germany, manufacturing outperformed expectations and held above 50 for a fourth consecutive month, though the pace of private-sector growth slowed.
Chris Williamson, chief business economist at S&P Global Market Intelligence, cited the resurgence of inflationary pressures as the main cause of the overall slowdown. Input cost inflation has accelerated for two consecutive months, and he explained that "in manufacturing, cost inflation has surged amid higher energy prices, and companies are raising selling prices to protect margins."
Energy, fuel and transport costs are the push factors. However, the pace of selling-price increases was slower than in September, suggesting that corporate margins are gradually coming under pressure. Williamson also noted that the effects of higher interest rates are beginning to weigh on demand. He said the situation of "growth continuing while inflation remains elevated is likely to strengthen expectations that the European Central Bank (ECB) will tighten more aggressively."
Among the main components, the flash services PMI fell to 51.7 from 53.0 in September, a two-month low. The manufacturing PMI dropped to 52.4 from 52.9. The manufacturing output index used to calculate the composite PMI also fell to 52.4 from 53.6, a four-month low. New orders rose for a fourth consecutive month, but at the weakest pace in that period. Meanwhile, new export orders increased for a third straight month, recovering from monthly declines that had persisted for about four and a half years. The growth rate exceeded that of total new orders. Employment was roughly flat, weighed down by slower growth in services and a slight decline in manufacturing.
Eurozone business sentiment sank to a five-month low, with optimism retreating sharply, particularly in manufacturing.
Rory Fenessey of Oxford Economics said the October flash reading poured cold water on the Eurozone economy, which had defied expectations from spring through summer. He said France's unstable situation is weighing heavily on the entire region, and government borrowing costs are rising further amid worsening fiscal conditions.
Concerns also remain strong in the market that a prolonged Middle East situation and the recent sharp rise in bond yields will weigh on activity. The ECB has already raised rates twice in response to high inflation and the energy shock and has signaled room for further tightening. However, the prevailing view is that it will hold policy rates at next week's meeting.
Harry Chambers of Capital Economics analyzed that while manufacturers continue to feel the squeeze from higher energy prices, evidence of second-round effects on wages and prices remains scarce. He indicated that this would be reassuring for the ECB.
Outside the Eurozone, the UK moved in the opposite direction. The UK PMI showed business activity at its highest level since February, maintaining firmness, but September retail sales (volume basis) released by the UK Office for National Statistics (ONS) fell 0.4% month-on-month, a sharper drop than market expectations.
Caution is also smoldering among some investors that a selloff in French government bonds could escalate into a Eurozone debt crisis. A bond investment chief at one asset management firm warned this week that it could become more serious than the crisis more than a decade ago.
PMIs are released early each month and are closely watched by the market as indicators that capture turning points in the economy early. However, because they measure the "breadth" of output changes, they may not directly correspond to quarterly gross domestic product (GDP).

New Delhi: India’s exports of goods and services to Germany could exceed $50 billion by 2030 through greater utilisation of the India-EU Free Trade Agreement (FTA) and deeper economic cooperation, according to a report released by Commerce and Industry Piyush Goyal.
According to a report of the industry chamber ASSOCHAM -- that was released by the minister in Berlin during his Germany visit -- noted that the India-EU FTA is expected to give bilateral trade fresh momentum.
“With the EU set to offer zero-duty access to a significant share of Indian exports, sectors such as textiles, apparel, leather, footwear, gems and jewellery, marine products, engineering goods, pharmaceuticals and electronics could benefit,” it added.
ASSOCHAM President Nirmal K. Minda said that India and Germany can leverage their respective strengths in manufacturing, technology and innovation to deepen economic cooperation and unlock new growth opportunities.
“Deeper industry engagement can create new opportunities for businesses, particularly MSMEs, and strengthen long-term economic ties,” he added.
According to the industry chamber, Germany’s strong industrial sector and India’s growing manufacturing and services sectors offer new opportunities for cooperation in advanced manufacturing, semiconductors, digital technology, critical minerals and defence.
“Germany’s Green and Sustainable Development Partnership, alongside cooperation in renewable energy, green hydrogen, electric mobility and battery storage, can support investment, technology exchange and sustainable industrial development,” said Saurabh Sanyal, Secretary General, ASSOCHAM.
“Stronger business-to-business engagement, sectoral interactions and buyer–seller meetings can help translate the growing partnership into tangible commercial outcomes and wider participation by Indian industry,” he added.
SP Sharma of ASSOCHAM noted that India has tremendous potential for export growth with greater utilisation of the India-EU FTA and exports can even reach $60 billion (54 billion euro) by 2030.
“Greater cooperation in trade, investment and technology can provide a sustained boost to bilateral economic relations,” Sharma said.
ASSOCHAM said it will continue to facilitate industry engagement and knowledge-sharing to help Indian businesses explore opportunities in Germany and strengthen the India–Germany strategic economic partnership.

articles.title: How Ukraine must protect personal data to join the EU and where progress is stalling - Європейська правда
articles.summary: How Ukraine must protect personal data to join the EU and where progress is stalling  Європейська правда
articles.full_text:
This process is already underway, but progress has been very slow.
Where is progress stalling, and what does Ukraine need to do? Read more in the article by Ilona Sologub of Vox Ukraine: A neglected reform: how the EU protects personal data and why Ukraine is moving towards it so slowly.
Personal data protection in the EU is governed by Convention 108+ on data protection, the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR), the Digital Services Act, the Digital Markets Act, the AI Act and other legislation. These rules apply not only to companies based in EU member states, but also to companies in other countries that process the data of EU residents.
The EU’s modern personal data protection framework is considered one of the most advanced in the world, which is why other countries use it as a model.
The European Commission can also designate countries and organisations as providing a level of personal data protection equivalent to that of the EU. Currently, this list includes 16 jurisdictions and organisations, including Argentina, Brazil and Uruguay. Companies in these countries and the designated organisations do not need additional authorisations or separate contracts to exchange data with companies in the EU.
Ukraine must bring its legislation fully into line with the EU’s General Data Protection Regulation. This obligation is included in the first cluster of EU accession negotiations, which covers Chapter 23, "Judiciary and Fundamental Rights", and Chapter 24, "Justice, Freedom and Security".
Two relevant bills have been submitted to the Ukrainian parliament but have yet to be adopted: Bill No. 8153 on personal data protection, introduced in 2022, and Bill No. 6177 on establishing a national commission for personal data protection, introduced in 2021.
Bill No. 8153, which passed its first reading in late 2024, proposes, among other measures, introducing a requirement for explicit and informed consent to the processing of personal data, as well as giving individuals the right to amend and delete their data.
The bill also proposes significantly increasing penalties for personal data protection violations. Currently, fines range from UAH 1,700 to UAH 34,000. Under the proposed legislation, they could reach UAH 90 million or 5% of a company’s annual turnover.
Under Ukraine’s National Programme for Adapting Legislation to the European Union Acquis, Bill No. 8153 was supposed to be adopted by June 2026.
However, Ukrainian media outlets and companies operating in the EU market are already required to comply with the GDPR. For the latter, the Ukrainian Ombudsman, who currently oversees personal data protection, has developed a series of recommendations on cross-border data transfers.
Another step Ukraine must take before joining the EU is to establish a national regulator for personal data protection.
Bill No. 6177 proposes creating a National Commission for Personal Data Protection and Access to Public Information, consisting of seven members appointed by the Cabinet of Ministers through a competitive selection process. Compliance with personal data protection rules would be monitored directly by the Commission’s Inspectorate Service, whose head would be appointed by the Commission’s chair following a competitive selection process.
Other tasks include bringing restrictions on access to internet resources into line with European freedom of expression standards. In particular, Ukraine needs to increase the transparency of decisions to block websites. It must also align the use of facial recognition and similar technologies, as well as its national e-Health system, with European data protection standards.
Ukraine’s open data framework must also be brought into line with the Open Data Directive and the Data Governance Act.
Artificial intelligence must not be overlooked either. Ultimately, Ukraine will also have to implement the EU AI Act as part of its accession process.

articles.title: Eurozone business activity slowed as France unrest weighs - The Business Times
articles.summary: Eurozone business activity slowed as France unrest weighs  The Business Times
articles.full_text:
However, at 51.9, the composite PMI is above the 50 threshold separating growth from contraction
Sudeshna Dhar
THE euro area’s private sector slowed more than expected in October, weighed down by France as the region’s No 2 economy grapples with fiscal and political tensions.
The composite purchasing managers’ index compiled by S&P Global decreased to 51.9 from 53.1 in September, though remained well above the 50 threshold separating growth from contraction.
Analysts in a Bloomberg survey had anticipated a smaller decline to 52.7.
While France performed significantly worse than expected, Germany recorded a fourth straight month above 50, underpinned by a stronger-than-anticipated performance by manufacturers.
“A key drag on growth was a renewed drop in business activity in the French service sector,” Chris Williamson, chief business economist at S&P Global Market Intelligence, said on Friday (Oct 23), adding that this “may be linked to strikes and unrest having disrupted some local economies”.
Even so, October activity for the wider region is “among some of the best performances seen over the past three years”, he added.
The euro-area economy has shown resilience to the Iran war and the accompanying energy-price shock, which along with above-target inflation has prompted the European Central Bank (ECB) to raise interest rates twice and signal more tightening may still be needed.
There is also concern, however, that the continued fighting in the Middle East and the recent jump in bond yields will weigh on economic activity.
Officials are widely expected to keep borrowing costs unchanged at the Oct 28 to 29 meeting.
David Powell, senior euro-area economist, said: “The composite PMI survey for the euro area suggests the bloc’s economy is beginning to weaken under the weight of higher commodity prices and tighter financial conditions.
“We think that double whammy will almost certainly cause the ECB to leave rates unchanged in October and end the hiking cycle after one final increase in December.”
Some investors and economists even see a risk that the rout in French bonds escalates into another euro-area debt crisis, with Franklin Templeton’s fixed-income investment chief on Wednesday warning it could end up being worse than the last more than a decade ago.
Turning to inflation, Williamson said input costs are rising sharply again, causing firms to push selling prices higher in order to protect margins.
“The picture of sustained growth and stubbornly elevated inflation from the October flash PMI will likely add to further speculation of more aggressive policy tightening from the ECB,” Williamson said. Higher borrowing costs have already started taking a toll by dampening demand, he added.
PMIs are closely watched by markets, as they arrive early in the month and are good at revealing trends and turning points in an economy.
A measure of breadth of changes in output rather than depth, business surveys can sometimes be difficult to map directly to quarterly gross domestic product. BLOOMBERG

articles.title: Starlink restrictions not lifted in Ukraine despite Trump's claims, defence officials say - Euronews.com
articles.summary: Starlink restrictions not lifted in Ukraine despite Trump's claims, defence officials say  Euronews.comUkraine says Starlink still restricted after Trump says limits lifted  BBCTrump, Musk, Zelenskyy: who is blaming whom in the Ukraine-Starlink row?  The GuardianWho actually controls Ukraine's access to Starlink?  BBCOpinion | Elon Musk is trying to make himself more powerful than the government  MS NOW
articles.full_text:
Ukrainian forces continue to experience disruptions to critical battlefield communications despite Donald Trump's assertion that restrictions have been removed, raising fresh questions about Kyiv's dependence on an American-controlled satellite network.
Restrictions on Starlink and its military-grade version, Starshield, have not been fully lifted along Ukraine's front lines, Ukrainian defence officials said on Friday, despite US President Donald Trump's claim that Elon Musk had removed them.
Officials monitoring the systems said they continued to record instances of terminals losing connectivity when travelling at speeds of 161 kilometres per hour.
Serhii Beskrestnov, an adviser to President Volodymyr Zelenskyy known by his call sign Flash, confirmed that the restrictions remained in place.
"We are currently seeing no indication that the Starlink restrictions have been lifted," he wrote on Facebook on Friday.
"There are isolated cases when Starlink can operate at speeds slightly above the limit, but this is probably due to SpaceX's algorithms or particular conditions of use, rather than the restrictions being removed."
The statements follow a report by The Wall Street Journal that Trump called Musk on 21 October to request that he lift the restrictions on Starshield, the military version of SpaceX's Starlink satellite communications service.
Following the call, American and Ukrainian officials reported improvements in connectivity, although some cautioned that full functionality had not been restored.
Trump subsequently claimed that Musk had removed the speed restrictions but declined to confirm whether he had personally contacted the billionaire.
The disruption began without warning on 14 October, when Starshield terminals used by Ukrainian forces started losing connectivity as they approached speeds of around 160 kilometres per hour.
The unexpected restrictions disrupted military operations, including mid-range strike drone missions and the use of interceptor drones deployed to defend Ukrainian cities against Russian aerial attacks.
More than a week later, responsibility for the decision remains publicly disputed. The Wall Street Journal reported that Musk had ordered the restrictions, while other accounts pointed to possible White House involvement. Trump has denied ordering the move, and neither SpaceX nor the US administration has publicly accepted responsibility.
The episode has exposed Ukraine's heavy dependence on Starlink, a critical component of its battlefield communications, drone operations and air defence, and the risks of relying on a satellite network controlled by a foreign provider.
Ukraine moves to reduce its dependence on Starlink
Ukraine is meanwhile seeking to develop its own satellite communications capabilities, in a move that could eventually reduce its reliance on SpaceX.
On Thursday, Ukraine's Defence Ministry signed a letter of intent with Finnish technology companies ICEYE and Nokia to explore cooperation on developing a sovereign satellite communications system.
Zelenskyy announced the agreement during Finnish Prime Minister Petteri Orpo's visit to Kyiv, describing it as "important for our defence and for the resilience of Ukraine".
The proposed systems would give participating countries ownership and control over their satellites, ground infrastructure and terminals, reducing their exposure to decisions taken by foreign governments or commercial providers.
"Ukraine needs secure, sovereign, and high-performance satellite communications systems that it controls," said ICEYE chief executive Rafal Modrzewski.
Mikko Hautala, chairman of Nokia Defense, echoed that message, saying the partnership would give Ukraine "control over the connectivity it depends on".
The agreement, however, remains at an early stage, leaving Ukraine reliant on Starlink for critical battlefield communications in the meantime.

articles.title: France slips into contraction as Europe’s growth slows: How bad could it get? - Euronews.com
articles.summary: France slips into contraction as Europe’s growth slows: How bad could it get?  Euronews.com
articles.full_text:
France’s private sector contracted this month, dragging eurozone business activity growth to a four-month low amid political uncertainty and high energy costs.
France's return to growth lasted just one month. Business activity contracted again in October, while confidence among French companies fell to its lowest level since the first Covid-19 lockdowns in 2020.
The drop pulled the wider eurozone down with it.
The eurozone's composite purchasing managers' index (PMI), which measures activity across manufacturing and services, fell to 51.9 in October from 53.1 in September.
It was the weakest reading in four months, although the index remains above 50, the threshold separating growth from contraction. Economists had expected a smaller decline to 52.7.
The services and manufacturing indices also came in lower than expected, albeit still signalling modest expansion.
The latest survey suggests Europe's recovery is losing momentum just as inflation is making it harder for the European Central Bank (ECB) to ease borrowing costs.
So is this a pause in growth, or the start of something worse?
What went wrong in France?
France recorded the sharpest deterioration among the eurozone's two largest economies. Its composite PMI dropped to 48.4 from 51.1 in September, well below the 50.5 economists had forecast.
The services activity index fell to 48.4, while the manufacturing index slipped to 49.3, its lowest level in 11 months.
Companies reported that customers were postponing projects and delaying spending decisions. New orders fell at their fastest pace since May, and export business declined for an eleventh consecutive month.
Employment fell too.
French businesses cut staff for the sixth month running, largely by leaving vacant positions unfilled and allowing temporary contracts to expire.
But the figures on business confidence were considerably worse. Expectations for the next 12 months fell to their lowest level since April 2020, when the pandemic had brought much of the French economy to a halt.
The survey also recorded negative business expectations for the first time in almost two years.
Joe Hayes, senior principal economist at S&P Global Market Intelligence, linked the deterioration to France's political and fiscal problems.
The sentiment reading, he said, "reflects firms' concerns about what is shaping up to be a highly uncertain 2027 Presidential Election, compounding pre-existing worries about France's fiscal situation."
France's political uncertainty has been accompanied by a sharp increase in government borrowing costs. That matters for businesses because rising interest rates make loans more expensive and can discourage investment, even without further ECB rate increases.
"Unsurprisingly, the volatile political situation and spike in government borrowing costs meant the downturn in the French composite PMI weighed on the overall picture," said Rory Fennessy, senior economist at Oxford Economics.
France had only returned to growth in September after months of contraction. The October numbers suggest that recovery has already run out of steam.
Is Germany holding up any better?
Germany offered a more encouraging picture, although growth also slowed.
The country's composite PMI eased to 52.8 from an 11-month high of 53.8 in September. Economists had expected 53.3.
Factories continued to expand. Germany's manufacturing PMI rose to 54.2, its highest reading in two months, supported by export orders and government spending on defence and infrastructure.
Services were weaker, with the index falling to 51.7. Companies in that sector reported that customers were delaying decisions and holding back spending as budgets tightened.
Phil Smith, economics associate director at S&P Global Market Intelligence, said the slowdown "underscored that the recovery in the eurozone's largest economy remains fragile."
Germany's factories also face a problem that could become more serious in the coming months. Manufacturers reported the fastest increase in input costs since May, particularly for oil, raw materials and electronic components.
Brent crude was trading near $114 a barrel on Friday, adding to the pressure on energy-intensive industries.
Confidence among manufacturers fell to its lowest level since July.
"A renewed surge in cost pressures has dampened expectations across the sector, with the two likely to remain intrinsically linked in the months ahead," Smith said.
Germany is benefiting from stronger factory orders, but companies are increasingly concerned about how much it will cost to fulfil them.
Why rising prices are becoming a problem for the ECB
The increase in costs extends beyond Germany. Across the eurozone, manufacturers reported higher prices for energy, fuel and transport, while supplier delivery times lengthened by the most in four months.
Chris Williamson, chief business economist at S&P Global Market Intelligence, said the survey still points to quarterly GDP growth of around 0.3%. But "higher interest rates are also starting to take a toll, dampening demand," he said.
With inflation remaining stubborn, Williamson said the figures "will likely add to further speculation of more aggressive policy tightening from the ECB."
That could mean higher borrowing costs for businesses and households, even as economic growth slows.
French stocks and bonds remain under pressure
France's CAC 40 fell 0.7% on Friday morning to around 7,750 points, more than 11% below its 10 August closing high.
Italy's FTSE MIB was broadly flat after Thursday's 2.5% decline, and is also down more than 10% from its August peak.
French government bonds have suffered an even sharper sell-off. The 10-year yield reached 5.14% on Thursday, its highest since 2002, before easing to around 5.04% on Friday.
The gap with German 10-year yields stood at 170 basis points, more than double the 78 basis points recorded in early August.
France now also pays around 45 basis points more than Italy to borrow for ten years. The euro was also under pressure, trading near $1.12, more than 4% below its August high.
A weaker euro can make imported energy more expensive, adding another source of inflation at a time when European manufacturers are already paying more for fuel and materials.
Is Europe heading for another recession?
The October business surveys are disappointing, but they do not yet suggest the eurozone is heading into recession.
There are, however, reasons to be cautious.
French companies are facing political uncertainty and rising borrowing costs. German manufacturers are struggling with higher energy prices, while businesses across the region are reporting weaker demand.
The ECB must now decide how much further it can raise borrowing costs to contain inflation without causing more damage to growth.
September's strong business surveys had raised hopes that Europe's recovery was finally gaining ground.
The October figures have called that into question, particularly in France, where companies are already cutting jobs and reporting their weakest expectations in more than six years.

French government bond yields eased in early trading, falling 3 basis points to 5.06%, but remained on track for their biggest weekly increase since late May. French 10-year yields have risen nearly 28 basis points this week, the largest increase among euro zone countries, reflecting mounting concerns over the country's fiscal outlook.
Read more: Japan’s Nikkei falls over 1% as Wall Street tech selloff rattles markets
Belgian 10-year yields have climbed 17 basis points this week, while Italian yields have risen 10 basis points. In contrast, German and Dutch 10-year yields have declined by 7.4 basis points and 6 basis points, respectively, highlighting a growing divide between countries with weaker public finances and those viewed as safer borrowers.
German Bund yields were little changed at 3.342% on Friday, while Dutch yields edged up 1 basis point to 3.452%. The divergence has pushed the risk premiums on French and Belgian government debt to their highest levels in well over a decade.
The broader bond market has been supported by a sharp rally in safe-haven assets, particularly US Treasuries, after renewed concerns about the profitability of artificial intelligence investments and their implications for global growth.
Read more: Safe-haven demand pushes Japan’s 10-year yield to two-month low
Investors are increasingly focused on whether companies developing and supplying artificial intelligence technology can generate sufficient returns on the trillions of dollars being committed to the sector. The resulting uncertainty has revived demand for government bonds as a portfolio hedge.
Central bank decisions in focus
Investors are also preparing for a series of major central bank decisions next week, with the US Federal Reserve, the Bank of Japan and the European Central Bank all expected to leave interest rates unchanged.
The ECB's policy outlook will be closely watched, particularly as rising French borrowing costs raise concerns about the potential for sovereign debt stress to spread across the region's financial markets.
According to Reuters, Deutsche Bank strategist Jim Reid noted that recent market stress had prompted fresh questions about the likelihood of further ECB rate increases this year.
Money markets had reduced the probability of an ECB rate hike by December to 69% on Thursday, down from 90% at Wednesday's close, reflecting growing doubts about the sustainability of further monetary tightening. However, LSEG data showed that the implied probability had recovered to around 80% by Friday morning.
Investors will therefore scrutinise ECB President Christine Lagarde's comments for clues about the bank's policy trajectory and its assessment of risks stemming from the French bond market.
The widening gap between French and German borrowing costs remains a key indicator of investor concerns about fiscal sustainability in the euro zone. While demand for safer government debt has helped stabilise broader bond markets, persistent pressure on France and other heavily indebted economies could keep sovereign risk firmly in focus in the coming weeks.
