There is no risk of power or gas outages during this winter in the UK, as there will be sufficient generation and gas supply, the National Energy System Operator has said in its early winter outlook.
In fact, NESO said it expected surplus electricity output at 5.5 GW for the period between October 31 and March 31 next year, “with an 8.8% buffer over expected peak demand.”
Things may yet change, however, the grid operator also said, noting factors to watch such as electricity generation in continental Europe, gas market developments, and the weather. NESO said the supply and demand situation is most vulnerable to unforeseen events in January.
Electricity security may be ensured for the winter, but it will not be cheap. Per Reuters, UK front-month gas and electricity prices are up by 180% and 120%, respectively, from February this year, before the war in the Middle East began.
The UK has become a lot more dependent on gas imports over the past decade or so, as it shrank its own production as part of decarbonization efforts. The island nation is also increasingly dependent on electricity imports from its continental neighbors, including France, Belgium, Denmark, the Netherlands, and Norway.
This dependence now exposes the UK to the European Union’s gas troubles: gas storage is barely above 70% full, and withdrawals have already started, ING commodity analysts wrote in a note earlier today. This may result in a supply squeeze down the road as the weather gets colder, even if the winter overall turns out milder than last year’s.
Despite that risk, the UK earlier this week reinforced this exposure, as Ofgem, the energy market regulator, approved a deal between National Gas and Interconnector Limited to keep the gas pipeline with Belgium operating, even at lower flows. These lower flows were the result of higher operating and maintenance costs, Reuters said in a report on the news.

Russian President Vladimir Putin said Thursday that future talks on ending the war against Ukraine should focus on security guarantees for both countries and an overall framework for security throughout Europe.
Putin, interviewed on Russian state television a day after meeting U.S. special envoy Steve Witkoff, confirmed that Russia was ready to resume U.S.-mediated talks with Ukraine next month.
He restated longstanding Kremlin policy that Russia never wanted to launch its full-scale invasion, but had run into hostile reactions from Ukraine on key issues of concern to Moscow.
Talks on a variety of matters could lead to a positive outcome, Putin said, but Russia remained intent on resolving the conflict once and for all rather than agreeing to a short-lived ceasefire.
"The goal of these talks will be to ensure the security of Ukraine and Russia after reaching peace agreements, in their final form, not as a result of a temporary ceasefire for some short period of time. We are ready to resume these contacts to achieve this goal," Putin said.
The Russian president said Witkoff also stressed that discussions had to extend to "the architecture of European security as a whole. And I agree with that too. Well, let's see how things develop in the coming days."
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky, who met Witkoff in Norway on Tuesday, said Ukraine was ready for talks likely to take place by early next month. Ukraine, he said, supported "any proposals for a ceasefire, an end to the war, an energy ceasefire as well as humanitarian initiatives."
The United States has led efforts to negotiate an end to the war in Ukraine, but talks have stalled since Trump ordered attacks against Iran in February.
Many of the disagreements about how to end the Ukraine war focus on territory, with Russia demanding Ukraine cede all of eastern Ukraine's Donbas region. Kyiv rejects any deal that would include giving up land it currently holds.
In his comments on Thursday, Putin said any discussion on territory in eastern Ukraine had to consider what he said was the fact that the area was "historically Russian land."
And residents there, he claimed, had voted to be a part of Russia in referendums staged seven months after Moscow launched its full-scale invasion.
"Firstly, my attitude on this matter is that this is not their territory. It’s the territory of historical Russia," Putin said.

First tanker loaded with Russian diesel is heading for New York after Moscow agreed to resume fuel exports to global markets under an arrangement reached between Russian President Vladimir Putin and U.S. President Donald Trump, according to LSEG shipping data.
The medium-sized vessel Agioi Fanendes took on 40,000 metric tons of ultra-low sulfur diesel at Russia’s Baltic port of Primorsk on Oct. 22. It is expected to arrive in the United States on Nov. 7, Reuters reported.
The agreement reverses part of the restrictions that have kept Russian petroleum products out of Western markets since the war in Ukraine began in 2022.
On Oct. 9, Trump announced that Russia would immediately supply more than 300,000 metric tons of diesel, equivalent to 2.25 million barrels, followed by another 500,000 tons in November and 1 million tons "immediately thereafter."
The U.S. Treasury Department also issued a sanctions waiver allowing the sale, delivery and import of diesel fuel, including into the United States, through April 7, 2027.
Moscow subsequently began relaxing its self-imposed export restrictions, allowing shipments to resume despite earlier efforts to preserve domestic supplies.
Russian Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak has indicated that the country could restore monthly diesel exports to between 3 million tons and 3.5 million tons by the end of the year, approaching its usual export volume.
The deal has drawn criticism from Ukraine and some U.S. lawmakers, who argue that renewed purchases provide Moscow with revenue despite its ongoing war against Ukraine.
Russia has shifted much of its diesel trade toward markets outside Europe since the EU’s full embargo on Russian oil products took effect in February 2023. Türkiye, Brazil and several African countries have become important destinations for its fuel.
However, Ukrainian drone strikes on Russian refineries have repeatedly disrupted fuel production, forcing Moscow to limit exports to protect domestic supplies.
The attacks have compounded the impact of refinery maintenance and other operational disruptions, leaving Russia with less diesel available for overseas buyers.
The International Energy Agency (IEA) reported that Russian refinery processing fell to 3.8 million barrels per day in June, its lowest level in more than 20 years and around 30% below the year-earlier level.
Diesel production was estimated to have declined by nearly 30% compared with 2025, prompting the government to restrict fuel exports to preserve domestic supplies.
Russian diesel exports averaged around 345,000 barrels per day so far this year, down 41% from the previous year, according to shipping data cited by Reuters.
Before the restrictions, Russia was one of the world’s largest diesel exporters, with monthly shipments of diesel and gasoil substantially higher than recent levels.

The European Union (EU) is “inviting disaster” by imposing a carbon tax on its steel products, Commerce and Industry Minister Piyush Goyal said in Berlin on Thursday (October 23, 2026).
Participating in the Berlin Global Dialogue, he also said the EU is “shooting” itself in the foot by bringing in more regulations, restrictions on itself, and closing its borders, something that actually helped them become a developed set of nations.
"You put a CBAM (Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism) on yourself. You put a 50% import duty to bring steel into your country. You're inviting disaster. Your cost of living will go up," he said.
He added that through this battery of regulations, the EU is trying to impose an artificial situation on itself, trying to create boundaries within Europe, trying to bring in "absolutely ridiculous" at times standards or levels of protection to safeguard certain sectors, steel being one of them, and only hurting its own economy.
"Now, imagine going forward, every infrastructure, whether it's a port or an airport or your autobahns in Germany or your expressways, your utilities, your water pipelines, you name the infrastructure with costlier steel, costlier aluminium, costlier cement, with all the overlay of CBAM and deforestation rules," he said.
He added that the EU has 75-77 regulations.
"We've lost count. You keep adding to your regulations, add to the burden of your industry, make yourself uncompetitive. And of course, in some sense, it'll also create non-tariff barriers for others to trade with you," Mr. Goyal said.
‘Reciprocal world’
He cautioned that the world is a reciprocal world now.
"And I don't say that. Much bigger leaders are saying that. And in this reciprocal world, you bring in a regulation and stop some other country from working with you. They'll bring in two regulations, which will hurt your businesses," he said.
He added that at the end of the day, cost of living in Europe will go up, business competitiveness will go down and inflation will be high.
"You will not be able to compete in global markets. Your auto industry is suffering that already. I think auto sales are down from Germany by 15 or 20% in the last decade or so," the Minister said, adding, "How will you be competitive in the future? You will ultimately outprice your industry."
He added that India is working on increasing competitiveness and is also working at a win-win partnership with everybody.
"We've got fair, equitable, and balanced agreements with every one of the partners with whom we are working. At least in the last four or five years, post-2014 particularly, we're forging friendships, basis competitiveness. We are building complementary strengths," he said.
He added that India would trade with countries such as Singapore, where there is no CBAM and deforestation.
India has raised concerns about these regulations on multiple occasions. Under the EU's Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM), Indian exports of steel, aluminium, and cement to the EU could face tariffs of 20-35%.
Mr. Goyal added that India accounts for only 3-3.5% of global carbon emissions despite supporting 17% of the world's population.
The European Union's anti-deforestation regulation (EUDR) is a form of a non-tariff barrier. The regulation imposes strict regulatory requirements on sectors such as rubber producers and exporters targeting European markets, as it is a non-tariff barrier.
Goyal said that the EU's contribution to carbon emissions is "humongous" and it is about 20%.
He noted that those nations used low-cost energy earlier to push through growth. But at present, India's contribution is low, and even the per capita damage to the ozone layer or carbon emission is probably 7-8 times lower than in Western nations.
The minister said that India has about 17% of the world population and it has the fastest clean energy programme.
"We are greening our steel," he said, criticising developed nations for failing to meet their climate finance and technology transfer promises to the developing and less developed countries.
He added that the CBAM does not recognise the principle of common but differentiated responsibilities.

articles.title: Russia strikes Kyiv with three cluster-warhead ballistic missiles, Zelenskyy says - Euronews.com
articles.summary: Russia strikes Kyiv with three cluster-warhead ballistic missiles, Zelenskyy says  Euronews.comRussia bombards Kyiv with missiles hours after agreeing to resume talks with Ukraine  The GuardianRussia bombards Ukraine after Trump envoy hails ‘humanitarian’ Putin  The TimesRussia and Ukraine trade fresh strikes despite renewed push for U.S.-brokered peace talks  CNBCRussia bombs Kyiv and Ukraine fires drones towards Moscow, despite talk of renewing negotiati...
articles.full_text:
The latest Russian bombardment of Ukraine's capital came just hours after US envoy Steve Witkoff met Vladimir Putin in St Petersburg, underscoring the stark contrast between Washington's renewed diplomatic efforts and Moscow's continuing attacks on Ukrainian cities.
Russian forces struck Kyiv overnight with three ballistic missiles carrying cluster warheads designed to inflict maximum casualties across densely populated areas, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy confirmed on Thursday.
One of the missiles struck Pechersk, the Ukrainian capital's historic centre, hitting an area between the Kyiv-Pechersk Lavra and the Holy Presentation Monastery, damaging religious buildings, homes, shops, cafés and other civilian infrastructure.
The missiles were designed to detonate in the air as they approached their targets, dispersing explosive submunitions across an area 400 metres in diameter, Zelenskyy said.
Serhii Beskrestnov, Ukraine's presidential adviser known by his callsign "Flash", earlier identified one of the missiles as an Iskander equipped with a K5 cluster warhead.
At least two dead and dozens injured
"This warhead detonates above the ground and is used specifically for inflicting maximum harm to people and equipment over an area of 400 by 400 metres," Beskrestnov said, adding that its 58 bomblets explode in the air.
Zelenskyy accused Moscow of deliberately targeting civilians in Kyiv's historic centre, insisting that the choice of both weapon and location was intentional.
"This is another extraordinarily revealing strike – revealing because it was no accident. The choice of weapon was deliberate, the choice of target area was deliberate, and so was the intent to inflict as much loss and damage on civilians as possible," he said.
"There was no military target nearby, not even in theory, and the weapon was designed to cause widespread destruction."
The strike was part of a large-scale Russian aerial assault on the Ukrainian capital and surrounding region overnight on 21–22 October.
At least two people were killed and 34 others injured, including five children, across the affected areas, according to Zelenskyy.
The bombardment came in several waves, with ballistic missiles and drones striking residential neighbourhoods, transport facilities and medical infrastructure across the capital.
Kyiv authorities reported damage in the Holosiivskyi, Obolonskyi, Pecherskyi, Sviatoshynskyi and Dniprovskyi districts.
Ukraine's Air Force said Russia had launched 210 drones, including 110 jet-powered variants, alongside Iskander-M, S-400, Zircon and Onyx missiles.
Ukrainian air defences intercepted or suppressed 181 drones, including 87 jet-powered variants, while strikes were recorded at 32 locations and falling debris at another eight.
Zelenskyy said Russia had fired 21 missiles in total during three waves of ballistic strikes on Kyiv.
The attacks continued throughout Thursday, with further strikes reported in Kharkiv, Dnipro, Marhanets, Mykolaiv and Kherson, as well as several other regions. In Kharkiv, a commuter train was hit, according to the Ukrainian president.
Zelenskyy said Russia had carried out more than 170 strikes against critical energy facilities since 11 October, despite Ukrainian air defences intercepting significant numbers of drones and some missiles.
He warned that Ukrainian intelligence identified Russian priorities for further attacks in the coming weeks, accusing Moscow of exploiting delays in Western air defence supplies.
"Russia is clearly taking advantage of the slowdown in air defence supplies from our partners," he said, calling for the accelerated delivery of military assistance already approved by Ukraine's allies.
The overnight bombardment came just hours after US special envoy Steve Witkoff met Russian President Vladimir Putin in St Petersburg as Washington sought to revive negotiations to end the war.
During the visit, Witkoff described Putin as a "humanitarian", despite the Russian president being wanted by the International Criminal Court over the alleged unlawful deportation and transfer of Ukrainian children.
Zelenskyy said on Wednesday that Ukraine was ready to accept literally any form of truce, on any aspect of the war, that Russia would be willing to agree to.
But following the latest attacks, the Ukrainian president questioned Moscow's willingness to pursue peace.
"Russia has not changed the way it wages this war, and it is taking no steps that would signal a genuine desire to end it," he said.

articles.title: Freed US citizen Stephen Hubbard was tortured in Russian jail, former Ukrainian prisoners say - BBC
articles.summary: Freed US citizen Stephen Hubbard was tortured in Russian jail, former Ukrainian prisoners say  BBCDowning Street rejects Witkoff’s description of Putin as a ‘humanitarian’  The GuardianRussia, US say American Hubbard was not released in exchange for a Russian war blogger  ReutersHow Putin ‘the humanitarian’ tortured, then traded, his US prisoner  The TimesTrump weighs in after his envoy calls Putin a ‘humanitarian’  The Independent
articles.full_text:
Freed US citizen was tortured in Russian jail, former Ukrainian prisoners say
Ukrainians held alongside freed US prisoner Stephen Hubbard have said they witnessed him being beaten and humiliated by Russian guards during his four-year detention.
Dmytro Khyliuk first met Hubbard at the Novozybkov prison in Bryansk, not far from Russia's border with Ukraine, in September 2022.
"We heard it from the guards. They came during inspections and were asking: in which cell is the American? And then they used obscene words. They threatened him, they mocked him from the first days."
Ihor Shyshko also remembers Hubbard's arrival at the jail and says his nationality marked him out to the officers.
"It attracted such attention because they mocked him, forced him to learn the Russian language, sing the national anthem and repeat the rules of the prison schedule, which he could not read."
Hubbard was captured in April 2022, when Russian soldiers occupied the eastern city of Izyum, where he was living with his Ukrainian partner.
He was accused of serving in Ukraine's armed forces and convicted in a trial in Moscow before being sentenced to six years and 10 months. Shyshko and Khyliuk were held alongside Hubbard as he awaited trial.
Shyshko said he witnessed and heard Hubbard being beaten by prison guards and electrocuted with a stun gun.
"They beat him on the legs, on the back, on the arms," he said. "Of course, they didn't give him food, they didn't give him medical care. They kept him in the cold.
"He was always treated more harshly, because he was an American. They claimed he was a mercenary, and said 'let's beat him'."
Shyshko, a captured Ukrainian soldier, alleges Hubbard was subjected to sexual humiliation and abuse for the entertainment of the prison staff.
Accounts from the two former Ukrainian prisoners corroborate statements made by Hubbard's family that he was tortured in prison.
The 74-year-old was released by the Kremlin after four-and-a-half years, on the day US special envoy Steve Witkoff met Vladimir Putin in St Petersburg to discuss the war in Ukraine.
Witkoff praised the Russian President as a "humanitarian", despite the ongoing full-scale invasion and daily Russian attacks across Ukraine.
US President Donald Trump said he had asked Putin to free Hubbard during a phone call the week before.
Khyliuk, a journalist, was held in the earliest days of the invasion, when Russian troops advanced towards the capital Kyiv.
He said he knew Hubbard's health was declining over the months they were initially held in nearby cells because he heard his complaints and the guards calling him more often to see the prison doctor.
Khyliuk described broken windows and biting cold, with detainees using time out of their cells to huddle together in the bathroom for warmth.
"It was very difficult conditions in Novozybkov, worse than in the next prison. It was very cold there in winter, terribly cold," he said.
Both men encountered the retired English teacher again at their next prison, Pakino, where Shyshko says Hubbard's condition worsened.
"There was not a single spot on his knees or on his feet without rot," he said.
"Everything was rotten. We all had scabies. It was very, very difficult for him. I even bandaged him once at the medical centre, because the doctor didn't want to do it. He just couldn't do it himself, and I had to help. He was quite weak then and he almost couldn't move."
They detailed a harsh regime and a meagre diet of porridge, bread and potatoes, with a daily routine of beatings and humiliation, being forced to run or hold stress positions.
"There's a handler with a dog, who lets go so it can bite you on the buttocks, on the elbow, or bite your leg. Then these wounds fester very badly," Shyshko said.
Khyliuk claimed that soon after their transfer to Pakino, Hubbard was hidden to conceal his condition from a team of International Red Cross visitors.
"I would like to say that an international humanitarian organisation that receives a lot of funding could do better. They saw only what was shown to them and they were happy with that," he said.
The International Committee of the Red Cross said in a statement that "in any situation where the ICRC has been granted access, we request to see every individual and assess the conditions they are held in. We continue our discussions with parties to the conflict on this issue."
Khyliuk said Hubbard disappeared from the prison in 2024 and he thought he must have been released. Khyliuk was returned to Ukraine in August 2025 in a prisoner exchange.
He likened their treatment to the regime of Soviet leader Joseph Stalin.
"Russian captivity is a torture machine. From the first second of your detention, they do everything to suppress you, to intimidate you. This is torture in all its manifestations, from psychological to physical. Beatings, hunger, cold, lack of any information, lack of the opportunity to communicate even with other prisoners".
Khyliuk said he was pleased to see Hubbard finally released and heading to the US.
"I understand what it is like to be in terrible captivity. Moreover, it was not his war. He ended up in the wrong place and at the wrong time," he said.
But he described the timing as "shameful PR of the US president, who is losing votes in elections to Congress".
Shyshko said he hoped one day their torturers would face justice.
"Evil must be punished, and so it will be. I have hope for that".

articles.title: Christa Pike's lawyer gives update on her condition after botched execution - Metro.co.uk
articles.summary: Christa Pike's lawyer gives update on her condition after botched execution  Metro.co.ukFrom death row to a botched execution and back: A timeline of Christa Pike’s case  CNNExecution staff warned IV site might have ‘blown’ during Christa Pike’s execution attempt  NBC NewsOne in three Americans back second execution attempt after failed one, Reuters/Ipsos poll finds  ReutersChrista Pike 'speaking in full sentences' as major health update given after botche...
articles.full_text:
Christa Pike is now speaking in full sentences and walking with far less help just three weeks after surviving her infamous failed execution attempt.
The 50-year-old was given two doses of pentobarbital as the state of Tennessee tried to carry out her death sentence on September 30. She somehow survived and was taken to hospital, where she remained unconscious and needed a ventilator.
One of her lawyers told TMZ on Wednesday that her speech has improved considerably in recent days. Her mobility has also improved, allowing her to walk more independently as she continues her recovery in prison.
But medical staff are still monitoring her cognitive and psychological functioning. Her lawyer said it could take another month or longer to establish whether she has suffered any lasting damage or not.
Pike had been due to become the first woman executed in Tennessee in more than 200 years. She was sentenced to death in 1996 for torturing and murdering her 19-year-old classmate, Colleen Slemmer, the previous year.
Both were students at the Job Corps Centre in Knoxville. Pike was 18 when Slemmer was killed on January 12, 1995.
Prosecutors said Pike believed Slemmer was interested in her boyfriend, Tadaryl Shipp. Slemmer was attacked near the University of Tennessee’s agricultural campus, where she was beaten and stabbed before Pike struck her head with a large piece of asphalt.
More than three decades later, Pike was taken to the execution chamber at Riverbend Maximum Security Institution in Nashville. Her lawyers say that the team carrying out the lethal injection repeatedly struggled to establish access to a vein.
According to a court filing from her legal team, at least seven needles were used during the attempt. One was bent at a 90-degree angle when it was removed, the filing said.
Her lawyers said she could be heard crying, whimpering and breathing loudly during the procedure. They reported that both her arms were swollen, burned and blistered when she arrived at hospital.
Pike’s legal team said they were subsequently told that she was totally brain dead and would soon be taken off life support. On October 6, however, she regained consciousness and began speaking.
Her lawyer Randy Spivey said that ‘to the shock of everyone, including me, including her team and including the medical team, Christa woke up and began talking’.
According to Spivey, her first words were: ‘Where am I and who are you?’
He said she also asked about Slemmer’s family.
Pike’s lawyers reported that she suffered pneumonia, a blood clot in her arm and difficulty eating following the execution attempt.
Spivey described ‘extraordinary’ swelling in her hands, saying they ‘looked like if you were to blow up a surgical glove’.
She was discharged from hospital on October 10 and transferred back to prison to continue receiving the necessary medical care.
Tennessee governor Bill Lee halted the state’s remaining executions for the year following the high profile botching of Pike’s execution.
Former US attorney Ed Stanton has been appointed to carry out an independent review into what happened.
The state’s prison chief, Frank Strada, also resigned in the aftermath. He said that stepping down while the review was conducted was ‘in the best interest of Tennesseans’.
Pike’s lawyers have urged Lee to commute her sentence to life imprisonment without the possibility of parole, preventing another attempt to execute her. They argue she has ‘endured punishment greater than any other person in the history of the American death penalty’.

articles.title: Boom in weight-loss drugs could lead to fall in beer sales, Heineken warns UK pubs - The Guardian
articles.summary: Boom in weight-loss drugs could lead to fall in beer sales, Heineken warns UK pubs  The GuardianHeineken urges pubs to sell half-pints to cope with fat jabs  The TelegraphEXCLUSIVE: Heineken document reveals worries over weight-loss drugs and beer sales  ReutersHeineken tells pubs to sell half-pints as GLP-1s bite  B2B NewsWhy Weight-Loss Drugs Could Change Your Next Round of Beer  Open Magazine
articles.full_text:
Heineken has warned British bars and pubs that the boom in popularity of weight-loss drugs could lead to a fall in sales of beer and cider.
The world’s second-largest brewer sent a presentation to British hospitality customers earlier this month that said the use of GLP-1 medication – such as Ozempic and Wegovy – could reduce the desire to drink alcohol. This in turn could result in “fullness and fewer serves” of pints in pubs and bars, it added.
The document, revealed by Reuters, said the GLP-1 era could lead to the tradition of the multi-pint drinking session becoming a less frequent occurrence.
The Netherlands-headquartered company offered advice including promoting half pints, low- and zero-alcohol options and pairing drinks with small plates of food, or risk declines in customer visits and spending.
“We see some changes in consumption behaviour among (GLP-1) users and will continue to monitor how these behaviours evolve in 2027,” said a Heineken spokesperson. “Consumer behaviour is evolving in response to a range of broader trends. GLP-1 is one of the developments we are monitoring.”
GLP-1 use has soared as consumers seek a quick solution to weight loss, with 10 million people turning to medication in the US last year, according to research by JP Morgan.
Heineken said the presentation was shared with customers as part of its regular engagement with UK businesses to help them understand how consumer habits were evolving.
Trends the brewer has identified in GLP-1 users include opting for smaller serves, lower alcohol drinks and more premium products.
“Our latest consumer research suggests GLP-1 users are not simply replacing alcohol,” said the spokesperson. “They are becoming more purposeful in their choices and broadening their preferences. These behaviours are not unique to GLP-1 users. They reflect broader consumer trends towards health and wellbeing, moderation, choice and more intentional consumption that we are seeing across our markets.”
As well as its eponymous lager, Heineken also owns brands such as Amstel, the Mexican lager Sol and Strongbow cider.
The Guinness maker, Diageo, has told investors that any impact from GLP-1 drugs becoming mainstream should be manageable, while Carlsberg told Reuters that data did not support the view that the use of weight-loss drugs affected beer consumption trends.
However, surveys by research companies including Circana, NIQ and KAM have pointed to reduced drinking by GLP-1 users.

Five Crucial Questions for the ECB Meeting Amid Inflation and French Bond Risks
Key Issues Facing the European Central Bank Ahead of October Meeting
By Dhara Ranasinghe and Stefano Rebaudo
LONDON, Oct 23 (Reuters) - The European Central Bank meets on Thursday against a backdrop of upheaval in France and an Iran war that is keeping energy prices above $100, meaning inflation risks remain elevated.
"How do you set rates against that backdrop? It's incredibly difficult," David Coombs, head of multi-asset investments at Rathbones Asset Management, said.
Here's a look at five key questions for markets ahead of the October meeting.
1. What will the ECB do?
ECB Rate Decision and Market Expectations
Leave its key interest rate unchanged at 2.5%.
A pause is widely anticipated after the ECB raised rates in June and September to counter rising inflation, as the Iran war pushed up energy prices.
Economists polled by Reuters expect a quarter-point rate hike in December.
"I don't think they've become materially less worried about inflation here," MUFG senior economist Henry Cook said.
2. What will the ECB say about the rate outlook?
ECB Guidance and Economic Concerns
It's likely to stick with a data-dependent approach.
Caught between high inflation, at 3.8% in September, and concerns that rising government bond yields could hurt growth, policymakers have recently argued for what ECB President Christine Lagarde called a "measured response."
"There will be a definite flag to the tightening in financial conditions and how it should slow growth and hence curb inflationary pressures," said Barclays' head of euro rates strategy Rohan Khanna.
"But also, plenty of uncertainty around the conflict and the outlook for energy prices."
3. How worried is the ECB about an energy-driven inflation rise?
Energy Prices and Inflation Risks
Comments from officials such as ECB chief economist Philip Lane suggest the ECB is not overly worried, for now, about high energy costs leading to other prices and wages rising.
A muted increase in core inflation, which excludes food and fuel prices, to 2.5% last month from 2.4%, suggests that high energy costs have yet to generate the sort of second-round impacts that could set off a hard-to-break inflation spiral.
Still, with oil up almost 80% this year and headline inflation above its 2% target, the ECB will likely stress vigilance.
Potential for Further Rate Hikes
"If the war in Iran escalates, or if we see further pressure on energy prices, the risk is still more rate hikes in 2027," said Bas van Geffen, senior macro strategist at Rabobank, adding he did not have any penciled in for next year.
Markets price in at least two hikes by mid-2027.
4. What about the French bond selloff?
French Bond Market Turmoil and ECB Response
Well, the ECB is watching.
French 10-year borrowing costs just hit 24-year highs above 5% and a weakened government is grappling with violent protests that could undermine efforts to improve fragile finances.
Also, the premium investors demand to hold 10-year French bonds over safer Germany is at 170 bps, up from 92 bps when the ECB met last month.
But don't expect the ECB to act soon with measures such as the Transmission Protection Instrument that allows it to buy bonds from any member state experiencing an "unwarranted, disorderly" tightening of its financing conditions.
France should solve its own debt problems through fiscal consolidation, says Lagarde.
Contagion Risks and ECB Policy Tools
The ECB could hold back on rate hikes if it thinks a crisis in France could hurt economic growth materially, Berenberg chief economist Holger Schmieding said.
"If there are serious contagion effects from a hypothetical French crisis to other countries where the fiscal policy is much more sustainable, the ECB would probably use its TPI to shield these other countries, not France," he said.
5. Who will replace Lagarde?
ECB Leadership Succession
The ECB chief, who could be appointed as the next World Economic Forum chair as early as November, will likely be pressed on succession.
The former central bank governors of the Netherlands and Spain, Klaas Knot and Pablo Hernandez de Cos, are seen as frontrunners.
Lagarde's exit would open a second vacancy on the ECB's six-member Executive Board after Isabel Schnabel's recent resignation. Chief economist Lane is meanwhile due to step down in May.
Timing and Political Implications
Lagarde's term is scheduled to end next October. Leaving early allows time for a new ECB chief to be picked before France's spring presidential election. A snap Spanish election could also impact the politics around ECB succession, analysts said.
(Reporting by Dhara Ranasinghe in London and Stefano Rebaudo in Milan; Editing by Toby Chopra)

Roula Khalaf, Editor of the FT, selects her favourite stories in this weekly newsletter.
Rolls-Royce is closing in on a deal for British taxpayer subsidies of up to £200mn to help fund the development of a new engine for short-haul aircraft, with an agreement potentially being announced as early as next week.
The investment would mark one of the biggest financial commitments by UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham towards his promise to reindustrialise the country and create thousands of new jobs in high-value manufacturing.
The support package of between £100mn and £200mn will help to fund the development and testing of a demonstrator model of Rolls-Royce’s new UltraFan 30 engine, according to two people briefed on the situation.
Negotiations between the two sides were still ongoing, according to one of the people, who cautioned that the timing of an announcement could yet change.
The FTSE 100 group has been pressing the government for more than a year about taxpayer support for its bid to re-enter the lucrative market for narrow-body aircraft such as the Airbus A320 or Boeing 737, which typically fly on short-haul routes.
Executives had hoped to secure an initial commitment towards the high-profile project in the first half of the year but an agreement was in part held up by the departure of Sir Keir Starmer as prime minister.
Burnham has made reindustrialisation of the UK a key priority since taking office in July.
Tufan Erginbilgiç, Rolls-Royce’s chief executive, has said the project could be a once-in-a-generation opportunity that could create as many as 40,000 skilled jobs, both at the company and in the wider supply chain, and generate as much as £120bn for the UK economy over the decades-long lifetime of the programme.
The development of a fully certified aircraft engine ready to go into production could cost up to £3bn, with additional funding needed for full-scale manufacturing.
The research and technology money for the demonstrator is expected to come via Britain’s Aerospace Technology Institute, which allocates state funding for innovation in the industry.
Rolls-Royce and the Department for Business, Science, Innovation and Trade both declined to comment.
Rolls-Royce has previously received UK government backing for engine programmes, including research and development funding and launch support.
Erginbilgiç, who has driven a sharp turnaround of the group since taking the helm in 2023, defended the company’s request for state aid in February after unveiling plans to return up to £9bn to shareholders over the next three years.
This type of state support was not uncommon in the industry, he said at the time, noting that his competitors — America’s Pratt & Whitney and GE Aerospace, and France’s Safran — received significantly greater sums.
The company would also invest substantial sums itself. An agreement with the government is expected to include commitments from Rolls-Royce on jobs.
The company had warned it could move production of the engine to Germany, where it builds business jet engines. It made the gearbox for the UltraFan programme at its facility in Dahlewitz, near Berlin, and some work is still expected to take place there.
Airbus and Boeing are expected to decide on engines for their next-generation narrow-body aircraft by the end of the decade, a lucrative opportunity in a market that Rolls-Royce left more than a decade ago to concentrate on wide-body planes.

Scope: This dossier assesses Italy’s manufacturing position within the European Union, with separate German, French and British comparisons, using evidence available by 22 October 2026 and a strategic horizon extending to 2036.
Executive Summary / BLUF
Italy’s manufacturing position remains substantial, but preserving its European ranking requires converting industrial specialisation into sustained productivity growth.
A comparable 2023 structural benchmark records approximately €321 billion in manufacturing value added and 3.91 million persons employed, against €774 billion and 8.16 million in Germany, and €291 billion and 3.26 million in France. documenti.camera.it
Confindustria identifies Italy as the world’s eighth-largest manufacturing economy and reports exports equivalent to 48.2% of manufacturing output in 2023. These are dated measures, rather than an undifferentiated 2026 baseline. Confindustria
Assolombarda’s October 2026 survey establishes accelerating AI project activity in its territory; it does not establish nationwide manufacturing adoption or realised productivity gains. assolombarda.it
The central policy requirement is coordinated investment in production data, workforce capabilities, automation, affordable electricity and supplier integration.
The decisive uncertainty is whether adoption spreads through industrial supply chains or remains concentrated among firms already equipped to invest.
Italy’s Factories Need Integration, Not Another Investment Announcement
Italy’s industrial policy faces a contradiction: it can finance more equipment without securing greater control over production. The Clean Industrial Deal State Aid Framework widens the scope for national support, while the Data Act changes access to industrial information and the Cyber Resilience Act turns connected products into continuing support obligations. Together, these instruments expose the weakness of an investment strategy measured chiefly through purchases and expenditure. Italy’s manufacturing position will endure only if public support and private capital connect machinery, engineering, qualified suppliers and operational control. Otherwise, taxpayers will help modernise factories whose critical inputs, software and customer relationships remain vulnerable to decisions taken elsewhere. The European consequence would be substantial productive capacity with insufficient resilience.
The numbers reveal a conversion problem
The financial evidence weakens the argument that Italian manufacturing primarily needs more credit. Confindustria’s 2025 report records an increase in own capital from 34.5% of manufacturing balance-sheet funding in 2007 to 48.9% in 2023. The EIB Investment Survey 2025 identifies financing constraints among 5.5% of Italian firms, against 6.1% across the EU, although its population extends beyond manufacturing. These aggregates do not remove individual financing difficulties. They suggest that stronger balance sheets and available funding can coexist with projects that firms cannot organise or execute.
The technological gap follows the same pattern. Official statistics assembled by Assolombarda put Italian enterprise AI use at 16.4% in 2025, compared with approximately 26.0% in Germany. Within Italy, adoption reached 53.1% among large enterprises but 15.7% among firms with 10–249 employees. These figures cover selected economic sectors, rather than factories alone. Their significance is organisational: the cost of combining technical expertise, usable data and management responsibility falls disproportionately on smaller businesses.
Equipment investment provides no automatic escape. Italy installed approximately 7,800 industrial robots in 2025, remaining the EU’s second-largest market, but installations declined by 11%. China installed approximately 354,000, an increase of 20%. Neither figure measures productivity. The longer record is more revealing: Confindustria reports growth in real manufacturing value added per hour of approximately 26% in Italy between 1995 and 2024, against around 80% in Germany and France. Italy has preserved substantial industrial capacity without matching its principal European competitors’ productivity improvement.
The skills pipeline also requires scrutiny. INDIRE’s 2026 monitoring records 9,991 ITS Academy graduates from courses completed in 2024, compared with 8,588 from courses completed in 2023. Yet employment within twelve months fell from 84.0% to 79.7% of graduates. Different cohorts prevent a causal judgment about programme quality. They nevertheless expose the distinction industrial policy must respect: expanding participation and improving outcomes are separate achievements.
A machine becomes productive only through an organisation
The EIB Investment Survey 2025’s relatively limited incidence of financing constraints makes project design more consequential. A manufacturer must pay for integration, qualification, training and disruption during installation, then maintain software and technical competence. An incentive that supports the purchase while leaving these costs unresolved can produce an installed asset without a functioning improvement in production.
The OECD’s December 2025 study of SME AI adoption illustrates the distance between experimentation and industrial change. In a representative survey cited by the study, only 29% of SME generative-AI users applied it to core activities. That is international evidence, not an Italian manufacturing estimate. Its relevance is the mechanism: cheaper administrative work does not establish better production scheduling, fewer defects or more reliable machinery.
The Made Smarter Adoption programme in England offers a useful organisational comparison because it combines expert advice, digital roadmaps, leadership development and grants. Its design recognises that technology diffusion requires managerial capacity. Italy’s corresponding test should be whether a smaller manufacturer can define a production problem, assess a supplier, retain responsibility after installation and reproduce the result across shifts or plants.
France 2030 supplies a further warning against premature declarations of success. The Direction générale des Entreprises’ October 2026 evaluation estimates that support raised total employment by 9%, R&D employment by 11% and productive fixed assets by 11% after two years in the evaluated early cohorts. It did not establish statistically significant effects on turnover or value added. Productive capacity can expand before commercial returns become measurable; evaluation must follow that sequence without confusing its stages.
European security depends on qualified output
Italy’s Catania semiconductor project shows what a capability-based policy can mean. The European Commission’s May 2024 decision approved approximately €2 billion of Italian support for STMicroelectronics’ €5 billion investment in integrated silicon-carbide production using 200 mm wafers. Its relevance lies in power devices for electrification and industrial applications. It cannot be interpreted as protection against shortages in every semiconductor category.
For the Catania project, the security return will depend on qualified output, technical performance, customer acceptance and dependable supporting supplies. An aid approval establishes permission to support investment; it does not establish that the intended capacity is operating commercially. Procurement and customer qualification transmit investment into resilience. Without them, Europe may finance facilities whose existence offers limited protection during an actual shortage.
The Net-Zero Industry Act applies the same question to a wider production system. Its benchmark seeks EU manufacturing capacity sufficient to meet at least 40% of annual deployment needs by 2030, while relevant procurement and renewable-energy auctions incorporate non-price considerations. For Italian suppliers, the commercial opening depends on satisfying the specifications buyers actually require. A European capacity target is not an order book, and equipment built for an obsolete specification remains commercially exposed.
The Critical Raw Materials Act further demonstrates why national production is insufficient. Its 2030 benchmarks distinguish extraction, processing, recycling and dependence on a single third country. An Italian factory purchasing through two European distributors may still depend on one upstream processor. Resilience requires tracing that common exposure and qualifying an alternative before disruption makes substitution urgent.
Digital control must survive a supplier’s departure
The Data Act, applicable since 12 September 2025, changes the bargaining relationship around connected machinery by establishing rules for access to generated data and switching between data-processing services. Italian equipment producers can use this framework to develop maintenance and optimisation services. They also face customers with stronger access rights and potentially more choice in the aftermarket.
The Data Act’s removal of provider switching charges from 12 January 2027 will not eliminate engineering costs. A manufacturer may retrieve files yet remain unable to recreate an application because its documentation, metadata or essential functions are tied to proprietary services. Operational control therefore requires a demonstrated migration or restoration capability. A contractual right that has never been tested offers uncertain protection when production is interrupted.
The Cyber Resilience Act makes the service obligation more explicit. Reporting requirements began on 11 September 2026, while the main obligations apply from 11 December 2027. Manufacturers within scope need continuing knowledge of their products’ software, vulnerabilities and support arrangements. For smaller industrial suppliers, this creates a fixed organisational cost that a machinery-purchase incentive does not resolve.

FICCI says MSMEs must upgrade product quality, meet European sustainability standards and integrate into regional supply chains to convert the India-EU free trade agreement into sustained export growth.
FICCI Secretary General Anant Swarup said the real challenge would be to convert improved market access into sustained market penetration.
He said that although the agreement, concluded in January, presents an unprecedented opportunity for Indian MSMEs to expand their presence in the European market, tariff concessions alone will not translate into higher exports.
Swarup is accompanying Commerce and Industry Minister Piyush Goyal, who is on a two-day visit here to boost trade and investment ties between India and Germany, its largest EU trading partner.
He said that MSMEs can also benefit by becoming suppliers to larger Indian and European companies, particularly in sectors such as textiles, leather, engineering components, chemicals and processed foods.
He noted that compliance with European standards will remain one of the most critical determinants of export success.
EU requirements relating to product safety, technical standards, sustainability, traceability and carbon emissions can be particularly challenging for smaller enterprises, he said, adding the EU's evolving regulatory framework, including CBAM (carbon border adjustment mechanism) and other sustainability-related requirements, will require Indian businesses to invest in cleaner technologies, certification and compliance systems.
Three areas of support will be particularly important: information and market intelligence, testing and certification infrastructure, and technology and financial support, he said.
He elaborated that industry needs practical, product-specific guidance on tariff concessions, rules of origin, regulatory requirements and export opportunities.
Dedicated FTA helpdesks, sector-specific advisory services and buyer-seller platforms can bridge this information gap.
"India must expand internationally accredited testing laboratories and certification facilities, particularly in major export clusters. Greater cooperation between Indian and European conformity assessment bodies can help reduce duplication, costs and delays," the Secretary General said.
MSMEs will need access to affordable finance, modern technology, digital traceability systems and support for meeting environmental and sustainability standards.
He added that shared facilities and targeted technology-upgradation programmes can make these investments more affordable.
"The FTA provides an institutional framework for regulatory dialogue and cooperation. This should be actively leveraged to address technical barriers, improve transparency and facilitate greater recognition of testing and certification systems wherever feasible," Swarup said.
He also said that Indian firms should look at the FTA beyond immediate tariff benefits as it can catalyse European investment into India, encourage technology partnerships, strengthen integration into global value chains and support diversification of our export markets.
"The real opportunity is not simply to export more to Europe, but to position India as a trusted manufacturing and services partner in European supply chains. This can deliver sustained gains in investment, production, employment and technological capabilities," he added.
India and the EU announced the conclusion of negotiations for the free trade agreement on January 27.
It is expected to be signed in December this year and may come into force next year.
India's exports to EU countries dipped by 4.57 per cent to $72.4 billion in 2025-26 from $75.85 billion in 2024-25.
These countries accounted for about 17 per cent of India's total merchandise shipments in the last fiscal.
Imports, on the other hand, rose by 9 per cent to $66.18 billion in 2025-26 from $60.68 billion in 2024-25.
These countries accounted for about 9 per cent of India's total merchandise imports in the last fiscal.
The trade gap was in the favour of India. Some of the European nations are major investors in India, and they include the Netherlands, Germany, France, Spain, Belgium, Italy, Sweden and Denmark.

articles.title: One interest rate, three inflation realities. Why Europe’s price shock is so uneven - Euronews.com
articles.summary: One interest rate, three inflation realities. Why Europe’s price shock is so uneven  Euronews.com
articles.full_text:
Finland, Germany and Lithuania share the euro and the ECB’s 2.50% deposit rate, but with September inflation at 2.7%, 3.3% and 6.1% respectively, they show how one policy meets different price realities.
Three countries share one currency and one central bank rate, yet their inflation rates differ by more than twofold.
In September, annual inflation was 2.7% in Finland, 3.3% in Germany and 6.1% in Lithuania, according to Eurostat’s harmonised index (HICP), published in October. The euro-area average was 3.8%. All three face the same European Central Bank (ECB) deposit rate of 2.50%.
An energy shock felt unevenly
The common thread is energy. Eurostat data show energy prices across the euro area rose 18.9% in September, adding 1.71 percentage points to inflation, almost half the headline figure. Excluding energy, euro-area inflation was 2.3%.
How that shock plays out depends on a country’s energy mix, tax choices and the strength of its domestic economy.
Lithuania: energy, taxes and wages
Lithuania sits at the top of the range, and food is not the reason. Eurostat figures show food, alcohol and tobacco inflation at 0.5%, while energy prices jumped 33.0% and services inflation reached 6.9%.
The International Monetary Fund (IMF) attributes the surge to elevated energy prices amid continued import dependence, strong domestic demand and higher excise duties. Policy added to the pressure. From January, Lithuania raised the VAT on residential heating, hot water and firewood from 9% to 21%. The government’s draft budget estimated that the heating change alone would add 0.5 percentage points to inflation.
Pressure has spread beyond fuel and heating. Eurostat data put Lithuania’s core inflation, excluding energy, food, alcohol and tobacco, at 3.9%. The Bank of Lithuania expects average wages to rise 9.4% in 2026, and the European Commission links services inflation to strong pay growth and an 11.1% rise in the minimum wage.
Higher wages may leave many workers better off on average. But pensioners, benefit recipients and low-income households with large energy bills are more exposed. There is also a second-round risk. Labour-intensive service businesses can pass higher wages into prices, keeping inflation elevated after the energy shock fades.
Finland: cushioned and sluggish
Eurostat figures show Finland faced a similar energy shock, with energy inflation at 13.1%, yet headline inflation stayed at 2.7%. The European Commission says Finland’s relatively low reliance on fossil fuels softened the blow. Statistics Finland found that cheaper electricity and owner-occupied housing costs restrained its national consumer price index, even as petrol, diesel and heating oil pushed it up.
Domestic price pressure is weak. According to Eurostat, core inflation was 1.4% and services inflation 1.7%. The Bank of Finland forecasts 10.4% unemployment in 2026, while the Commission expects GDP growth of 0.8%. Statistics Finland reports nominal earnings rose 3.5% year on year in the third quarter, or 1.2% in real terms.
That combination helps explain why another rate rise may seem overly restrictive from Helsinki.
Germany: a spike concentrated in fuel
Germany falls in the middle. Eurostat data show energy inflation at 13.4% and core inflation at 2.5%. Germany’s statistics office, Destatis, found motor fuels up 37.1% and heating oil up 74.9% in the national index. Excluding those two items, inflation was 1.8%.
Wage pressure is moderate. Negotiated wages rose 2.9% year on year in August, and the Bundesbank projects the same average for 2026. Eurostat puts services inflation at 2.8%.
Policy also muddies the picture. Existing federal measures lowered electricity, gas and district-heating prices, and a new fuel-tax cut took effect on 1 October, so it is not included in September’s figures. National interventions can shift measured inflation monthly without changing the underlying European shock.
What a single rate means
The ECB raised its deposit rate from 2.25% to 2.50% in September, arguing that the Middle East conflict was keeping inflation above target and that the full effects of the energy shock had yet to emerge.
Subtracting national headline inflation from the ECB rate gives a rough real-rate proxy: minus 0.2% in Finland, minus 0.8% in Germany and minus 3.6% in Lithuania. This simple calculation based on ECB and Eurostat figures is not a true measure, since households and firms act on expected inflation and face different borrowing costs.
The policy tensions differ by country. Finland’s weak growth and high unemployment argue against tightening. In Germany, the rate is easier to defend given core inflation of 2.5%, but September’s acceleration was driven almost entirely by fuel and heating oil. In Lithuania, the rate looks loose against 6.1% inflation, though higher rates cannot reverse a VAT increase or lower imported fuel prices. They work by weakening demand and curbing second-round effects.
Transmission also varies. ECB research finds that policy works faster and more strongly where variable-rate debt and household leverage are more common, and Lithuania is among the countries relying on variable-rate mortgages with short reset periods.
Yet a recent study covering 2000 to 2025 suggests output and inflation responses to monetary policy are less uneven than often assumed, as some structural differences offset each other.
Sources: Eurostat, ECB, IMF, European Commission, Bank of Lithuania, Bank of Finland, Statistics Finland, Destatis, Bundesbank.

Celebrity shark guided out of South Korea canal refuses to swim out to sea
A famed dusky shark in South Korea is still lingering near a canal that it was guided out of on Wednesday.
The shark, nicknamed Bukangi, became an unlikely sensation after it was spotted swimming in a canal in the south-eastern port city of Busan last month. For weeks, rescuers tried in vain to get it back to the open sea using large nets.
On Thursday, authorities said they had reinforced barriers to prevent Bukangi from returning. But it has yet to swim out into the open sea, and has been circling back repeatedly to the mouth of the waterway.
Its rescue prompted mixed reactions in Busan, where some said the shark should stay while others felt it was better for it to go.
In a livestreamed operation on Wednesday, rescue workers took more than eight hours to delicately guide the three-metre-long (10ft) shark with a net towards open water in a harbour.
Hundreds of adoring fans gathered at the park overlooking the canal, cheering and waving goodbye to the shark.
But then, on Thursday morning, Bukangi reportedly swam back into the canal after breaking through a barrier installed by authorities.
For some time, Bukangi was trapped in a tight space between two layers of nets in the canal.
Rescuers freed it by removing the outer layer, and have since fortified the remaining layer of nets to prevent it from going back in.
Since then, authorities said, Bukangi has been swimming further out but keeps circling back.
A government official told the BBC on Thursday afternoon that rescuers had concluded their operations to free the shark.
It is thought that Bukangi might have been drawn to the canal by unusually warm waters and plenty of fish. With the sea getting warmer each year, experts say Busan may play host to more sharks in the future.
In the month that she has been in the canal, Bukangi had already attracted more than 1.6 million visitors.
Its popularity gave a welcome boost to Busan's tourism, and the city embraced it as an unofficial mascot.
But authorities were also concerned about Bukangi's well-being as it appeared to be injured and was not eating.
Social media users have been circulating videos of Bukangi swimming in the canal with what appears to be a bloodied snout.
There were concerns the shark would be further weakened by falling water temperatures.
Before this week's operation, there had been two earlier failed attempts to guide Bukangi out of the canal with nets.
Some in Busan felt it was safer for the shark to remain in the canal. The BBC saw two people holding up cardboard signs protesting against Bukangi's eviction.
One of them was Cho Hannah, who had travelled for two hours from her home in North Gyeongsang province to see the shark.
Bukangi, she insisted, was "a rare gift" to Busan.
"This shark has made this canal her home, and we are kicking her out unnecessarily. I am afraid the shark might die tangled with the net, or die out at sea," she said.
But others like Yoon In-taek said it was only right that Bukangi left.
"Bukangi seemed much larger when I first saw her on 18 September, when she first got here. Now she seems gaunt. I'm worried for her health if she stays," he said.
"It doesn't sit right with me that she keeps returning here. It will be best if Bukangi leaves, doesn't come back, and lives and feeds freely in the open sea. I'd love to see her find a healthy, free life out there," said Shin Seungmin.
Bukangi has "brought so much joy to us", he said, adding that he was sad to see her leave.
"But she should go and live her normal shark life."

articles.full_text:
Welcome to Michael Kramer’s pick of the key market events to look out for in the week beginning Monday 26 October.
Published: Friday, 23 October 2026 at 12.30pm (UK)
It’s set to be one of the busier weeks of the fourth quarter, with the UK Budget announcement likely to be the domestic focus of attention on Wednesday afternoon. The Federal Open Market Committee’s (FOMC) US interest-rate decision is also due later that day, while mega-cap earnings season gets into full swing with big tech giants such as Microsoft, Amazon, and Alphabet all reporting.
US interest-rate decision
Wednesday 28 October
The market is not pricing in a US rate hike at the October meeting and instead expects the next increase to occur in December. Still, this doesn't mean the FOMC can't raise rates at this month's meeting. However, it appears highly unlikely, and would break with established market norms and expectations.
Nevertheless, a hawkish stance or hints of future rate hikes could rattle markets, particularly commodities like gold, which have already been weakening and are now closer to breaking below significant support around $4,000, a level that has been highlighted for some time. If gold finally breaks below $4,000, it could send prices back towards the mid-$3,000s, potentially targeting $3,600 as the next major support level.

Source: TradingView, 22 October 2026
Microsoft Q1 earnings
Wednesday 28 October
Microsoft is expected to report fiscal first-quarter earnings growth of 14.3% year-on-year to $4.72 a share, with revenue forecast to rise 16.8% to $90.1bn. Meanwhile, capital expenditure is expected to rise to $46.6bn from $19.4bn a year ago. For fiscal Q2, analysts expect earnings to grow 16.9% to $4.84 a share, with revenue up 17.6% to $95.6bn. Capital expenditure is expected to rise to $48.4bn from $29.9bn a year ago. The stock is expected to move around 4.7% after the earnings release.
Microsoft's option positioning is extremely bullish, suggesting that after the company reports results and implied volatility declines, hedging flows could weigh on the stock and create selling pressure. Additionally, option positioning shows a significant concentration of call gamma around $575, which may act as resistance, while put gamma indicates a strong support level around $495.
The technical chart shows that Microsoft's stock has moved back towards its all-time highs but has struggled to break above resistance around $550. This marks the third time since 31 July 2025 that the stock has tested that level and failed to break through. Microsoft’s share price is now showing signs of weakness, with support around $520.
However, if the stock continues its recent decline after the results, the next meaningful support is around $495, consistent with options market positioning. A break below that price could expose the stock to significant downside towards $475, or potentially as low as $465. The upside appears somewhat limited: the stock has repeatedly struggled to break above $550, while the significant concentration of call gamma around $575 could also provide resistance.
Microsoft share price, May 2025 – present
Source: TradingView, 22 October 2026
US PCE
Thursday 29 October
Unfortunately for traders and investors, the US September personal consumption expenditures (PCE) report will be released the day after the Federal Reserve’s meeting. It’s expected to be another hot inflation reading: headline PCE is forecast to rise by 0.5% month-on-month, up from 0.3%, while the year-on-year rate is expected to increase to 3.6% from 3.4%. Meanwhile, core PCE is expected to rise by 0.3% month-on-month, up from 0.2%, with the year-on-year rate increasing to 3.1% from 3%.
By the time Thursday’s PCE report is released, markets will have had time to digest the Fed meeting, and the inflation data is likely to add another layer to the market's reaction.
The euro remains vulnerable against the dollar, with EUR/USD sitting close to support around $1.12. If the Fed adopts a more hawkish stance, and the PCE report comes in hotter than expected, the euro could slide towards support around $1.10.
Conversely, if the Fed appears to be more tolerant of the inflation picture, while the PCE report comes in cooler than expected, the euro might rally. The euro-dollar pair could then break above resistance around $1.135 and may potentially move back towards its 50-day moving average, currently around $1.144.

articles.title: Piyush Goyal Urges Indian Diaspora in Germany to Boost Global Trade - Asianet Newsable
articles.summary: Piyush Goyal Urges Indian Diaspora in Germany to Boost Global Trade  Asianet Newsable
articles.full_text:
Union Minister Piyush Goyal has urged the Indian diaspora in Germany to help boost bilateral trade, investments, and export orders to strengthen India's global economic footprint through professional networking and commercial partnerships.
Piyush Goyal Seeks Diaspora Support for Global Trade
Union Commerce and Industry Minister Piyush Goyal on Friday called on the Indian diaspora in Germany to leverage its professional networks, business experience and local connections to facilitate investments, export orders and service contracts for Indian companies, as India seeks to expand its global economic presence.
Addressing members of the Indian community in Berlin, Goyal said overseas Indians could serve as a “living bridge” between India and Germany by helping Indian businesses access international markets and establish commercial partnerships. He said India was working to expand its economic engagement with other countries through free trade agreements and stronger economic and geopolitical partnerships, with the aim of increasing trade and strengthening the country's position in the global economy.
Strategic Growth and Manufacturing Ambitions
Goyal said India had the potential to expand its manufacturing scale and strengthen its services sector, adding that the country’s growth ambitions would require contributions from people both within India and abroad. “We cannot manufacture ambition. That ambition, that drive will have to come from the people,” the minister said, highlighting the role of knowledge, capital, networks and experience that the Indian diaspora could bring to the country's growth.
Trade Hub and Private Sector Participation
Proposed International Trade Hub
Responding to a proposal for an Indian International Trade Hub in Germany to help small businesses reach European customers, Goyal said the government could support the creation of an overseas warehouse managed professionally by an industry or community association. He said such a facility could allow Indian exporters to store goods in Germany and facilitate their sale in the local market, provided clear arrangements were made for financing, insurance, safety and security. The minister said the government could not directly establish such a warehouse but could extend support if an association took responsibility for its management and ensured fair access for exporters.
The Role of Private Enterprise
Goyal also said private-sector participation was essential for economic growth, citing India's information technology industry as an example of how businesses could flourish when the government acted as a facilitator without excessive interference.
Bilateral Trade Milestone
India's Ambassador to Germany Ajit Vinayak Gupte said bilateral trade between the two countries had reached a record USD 53 billion. He also highlighted the growing Indian community in Germany, which has crossed 332,000 people, and its contribution to science, technology, finance and other sectors. Gupte said the diaspora continued to play an important role in strengthening commercial and people-to-people ties between India and Germany.
