articles.title: Algeria Halts Urea Exports to France Amid Diplomatic Tensions - Global Banking & Finance Review
articles.summary: Algeria Halts Urea Exports to France Amid Diplomatic Tensions  Global Banking & Finance Review
articles.full_text:
Algeria Suspends Urea Exports to France as Diplomatic Rift Escalates
Escalating Trade Tensions and Their Impact on France
By Gus Trompiz and John Irish
PARIS, Oct 23 (Reuters) - Algeria has instructed urea producers to stop exporting the fertiliser to France in an intensification of trade curbs that have followed a diplomatic rift between Algeria and its former colonial ruler, according to diplomats and industry sources.
Ties between Paris and Algiers, which have been complicated for decades, deteriorated in 2024 when French President Emmanuel Macron backed a plan for autonomy for the Western Sahara region under Moroccan sovereignty.
The two countries sought to repair relations last year, even at one point declaring that the relationship was back to normal, but ties have since soured again.
Information about a halt to urea exports emerged early last week, French fertiliser industry association Afcome and wheat growers group AGPB said, noting that could put at risk around 30% of France's imports.
General Product Boycott and Trade Restrictions
GENERAL PRODUCT BOYCOTT
Three diplomats also said they were aware of an instruction by Algeria to suspend urea shipments to France. They were among six French and European diplomats who also said that Algiers had in late July imposed a near-blanket ban on French imports.
The diplomats requested anonymity to discuss the issue.
Any disruption to Algerian urea supplies could create fresh concerns for French farmers, who rely on nitrogen-based fertilisers to maintain crop yields and who have already faced higher costs.
The dispute could also become politically sensitive for President Emmanuel Macron's government, which is under pressure to shield households and producers from rising costs while managing a sharp deterioration in relations with Algeria, a topic that often polarises the French political landscape.
France experienced some of the worst unrest in years last weekend and a potential confrontation with farmers over fertiliser supplies could only add to that pressure.
Like with previous trade restrictions, including a halt to Algerian imports of French wheat since 2024, the sources said there had been no formal announcement by the Algerian government regarding either urea exports or imports of French goods.
The Algerian embassy in Paris did not immediately respond to emailed questions from Reuters. Algeria's trade and foreign ministries were also not immediately available for comment on Friday, a non-working day in the country.
France's foreign ministry said it had not received notification of such trade restrictions.
Trade matters were a competence of the European Union, it said, adding: "We will, of course, remain particularly vigilant on this issue."
France Raises Issue at the European Union
FRANCE BRINGS UP RESTRICTIONS AT EU
Two diplomats said France's Foreign Minister Jean-Noel Barrot brought up the broader ban on French goods by Algeria during a monthly EU foreign ministers' meeting.
"France referred to Algeria in the context of recently adopted trade restrictions on French imports," according to an EU summary of an Oct. 12 meeting.
The European Commission did not immediately respond to requests for comment.
Several diplomats said that Algeria had denied the curbs when asked by French representatives.
Trade Data and Economic Impact
Trade between the two countries has shrunk since 2024.
Total French exports to Algeria fell about 12% to €4.2 billion in 2025, and dropped by about 12% year on year in the first eight months of 2026, French customs data shows.
France's imports from Algeria, mostly oil and gas, declined by 18% last year to €5.1 billion and were down 11% for January-August this year.
Algeria's Hard Line Ahead of French Elections
ALGERIA TAKES HARD LINE AHEAD OF FRENCH ELECTIONS
The exact reasons for further restrictions on Algeria's trade with France were not clear.
Several sources saw a continuation of bilateral diplomatic tensions, given that the curbs targeted France rather than the EU, with which Algeria has a trade agreement.
Algiers might see an opportunity to take a harder line ahead of next year's presidential election in France, said Jalel Harchaoui, a contributor to Britain's Royal United Services Institute think tank.
Political Motivations and Regional Dynamics
"The risk is a new president who opens their term with a burst of anti-Algerian demagoguery, lashing out with something spectacular just for domestic political purposes," he said.
"Squeezing France ahead of time guards against that, since it’s always easy to ease the pressure later. It also costs nothing right now, because Macron is already a lame duck president, and a pro-Morocco, pro-UAE one at that."
Algeria last month cut diplomatic relations with the United Arab Emirates, which has also backed Morocco over the Western Sahara.
Rising Costs and Uncertainty for French Farmers
RISING COSTS FOR FARMERS
Supply Chain Disruptions
An interruption to shipments of Algerian urea to France could add to difficulties for farmers in the EU's biggest agricultural sector, after the Iran war disrupted fertiliser supplies from the Gulf.
Market Volatility and Future Outlook
A squeeze on Algerian supplies, as well as rising prices of gas, a key input for producing fertiliser, could push up costs for farmers as they start to cover requirements for next spring's growing season, said Cedric Benoist, the AGPB's deputy secretary general in charge of fertiliser issues.
However, it was too soon to tell if Algerian urea shipments were being impacted, Emmanuel Nizon, head of public affairs at Afcome, said, adding that flows fluctuate due to prices and other factors.
(Additional reporting by Philip Blenkinsop, Andrew Gray, Leigh Thomas, May Angel; editing by Sudip Kar-Gupta, Tomasz Janowski and Jason Neely)

articles.title: New storage markets change the game - EnergyTransition.org
articles.summary: New storage markets change the game  EnergyTransition.org
articles.full_text:
The ’battery revolution’ is transforming the debate over whether renewables can power whole economies. New battery storage options can be the backbone of a complex, decentralized, volatile grid. Paul Hockenos reports.
On the tiny neck of land connecting northernmost Germany to Denmark lies Germany’s largest battery, the pride of a German-Norwegian firm. Since last year, the three-acre site, surrounded by farmland, has hosted 64 gleaming white industrial containers arranged in symmetrical rows, housing over 200,000 South Korean–manufactured lithium-ion batteries. This volume can supply around 170,000 households with renewable electricity for two hours – valuable in a region that produces and relies heavily on wind power.
But battery storage is expanding so fast in Germany, and globally, that this facility will soon be dwarfed. One project in eastern Germany will soon keep the lights on in 1.6 million households for four hours. Even that behemoth – part of a ’gigawatt factory’ combining solar power, wind power, battery storage and hydrogen-capable gas plants – won’t be Europe’s record holder for long, as battery storage is expected to grow six-fold by 2030. Part of that growth, thanks to EU legislation, will come not from monster-size batteries but from models small enough to fit under a car hood or in a basement.
‘The quest for reliable, cost-effective electricity storage has long been seen as a holy grail for the power sector,’ says Toby Couture of E3 Analytics. ’Now, after decades of technological advances, accelerated by the economies of scale from mobile phones, we essentially have it. And it’s changing everything.’
Experts describe a ’battery revolution’ breaking over global markets, as utility-scale storage costs have collapsed while hardware capacity has surged. This shift is transforming the debate over whether renewables can power whole economies. ’Solar and wind energy, paired with battery storage, are reliable and already deliver cost-effective, round-the-clock electricity,’ concludes a new report from the International Renewable Energy Agency (IRENA).
’Over the last 25 years, we added renewables, renewables and more renewables that introduced incredible volatility, but we had few ways of balancing it out,’ says Eva Zimmermann of Aurora Energy Research. ’Our energy systems were still stuck in the age of fossil fuels.’
Until recently, critics could point to the intermittency of sun and wind as reason for doubt, warning of blackouts on overcast, windless days. Storage options – pumped hydro, compressed air, flywheels, green hydrogen, batteries and so on – were too costly or impractical. One of the transition’s central challenges is ensuring clean electricity is available whenever and wherever needed, not only when conditions are favourable.
This is why storage was long considered the ‘missing link’ for a renewables-powered world. Now it’s called ’the great enabler’.
’The long-standing argument that renewables lack reliability no longer holds,’ says IRENA Director-General Francesco La Camera.
’The new battery storage options can be the backbone of a more complex, more decentralized, more volatile grid,’ says Kai-Philipp Kairies, a battery expert and energy company founder. ’Every day our grids are getting more complex – for example with data centres. Batteries are keeping the lights on.’
Falling costs, rising stakes
Innovations in lithium-ion chemistry have driven battery storage prices down by as much as 93 per cent since 2010, and the decline isn’t over. The broader ‘electrification of everything’ – the shift from fossil fuel technologies to electric alternatives powered by renewables – has pushed prices down further.
Just as important, experts say, is the maturing of energy storage markets, once a niche component of power systems and now central to the global energy transition. In most places, pumped hydroelectric storage was the technology of choice, converting electricity into kinetic energy by pumping water uphill and releasing it on demand.
Zimmermann says EU legislation liberalizing energy markets arrived ’at just the right time’ – as Russia’s invasion of Ukraine sparked an energy crisis demanding more renewables online, fast. ’These new liberalizations enabled battery storage to enter the market and offer the grids exactly what they needed.’
A renewables-based system doesn’t just need more storage capacity – it needs more providers that can respond within seconds or minutes. This extreme volatility has driven the rise of faster balancing markets, such as ancillary services and grid stabilization measures like voltage control – matching supply and demand in real time in ways unimaginable five years ago.
Kairies, owner of ACCURE Battery Intelligence, which offers ancillary services, explains: ‘Grid operators pay generators to hold back energy and push it into the grid on demand – that’s been done with gas and coal plants for decades. Batteries do it better. They’re more dynamic, controllable at finer granularity, and their cost is a fraction of legacy players like gas, coal, and pumped hydro.’
’Battery storage can significantly reduce the need for expensive backup gas power plants,’ adds Carsten Körnig of BSW Solar, Germany’s solar energy association. ‘They can be built more quickly, produce no direct CO₂ emissions and reduce system costs by integrating renewable energy and alleviating grid congestion.’
Room for small players
Utility-scale battery farms will do the heavy lifting in balancing markets, but there’s room for smaller players too. EU legislation opened the market to ‘prosumers’, much as it did for household renewable energy producers decades ago. Germany leads Europe, accounting for roughly 70 per cent of residential storage capacity, driven by payments for feeding stored energy into the grid and subsidies covering up to 30 per cent of storage costs. The US is catching up, especially in California, Texas and Hawaii, where a 30 per cent federal tax credit applies to small-scale residential storage. Homeowners can earn hundreds to over $10,000 annually selling storage capacity to virtual power plants – companies that aggregate this flexibility to provide balancing services to grid operators.
In the UK, consumers are responding to the energy crisis by investing in batteries and other green solutions. ’For the right home, home batteries can cut bills, increase flexibility and make everyday energy use smarter and more resilient,’ says British energy expert Tom Pakenham.
Germany’s energy transition remains a work in progress. It aims to generate 80 per cent of its electricity from renewables by decade’s end, and the more wind and solar in the grid, the more fast-responding flexibility it needs. One German research institute estimates storage demand of 100 to 170 GWh by 2030 – against a current capacity of just 27 GWh.
IRENA’s report also urges caution. Lithium-ion systems provide only short-duration storage, it notes; higher renewable shares will require long-duration solutions, such as sodium-ion batteries, solid-state systems, iron-air storage and green hydrogen. The rollout also demands vast volumes of critical minerals, whose extraction carries well-known environmental and geopolitical risks.
Battery advances will drive another nail into the coffin of fossil fuels and nuclear power – but buildout must cover both existing renewables and those now entering the system. ’We’re still playing catch-up as the target moves ahead,’ says Zimmermann. In Europe, the first quarter of 2026 saw twice as many negative-price days as the same period in 2025. Catching up with its own renewables expansion by 2030 will take some doing.

articles.title: Telegraph cuts up to 100 jobs as new owner promises to turn paper into ‘AI-powered’ global business - The Guardian
articles.summary: Telegraph cuts up to 100 jobs as new owner promises to turn paper into ‘AI-powered’ global business  The GuardianAxel Springer to Cut Telegraph Jobs After Buying UK Newspaper  Bloomberg.comTelegraph cuts up to 100 jobs as it targets being ‘global, AI-powered’ business  Press GazetteAxel Springer to Restructure Telegraph as ‘Global, AI-Powered Media and Intelligence Business’  A Media OperatorAbout a Hundred Telegraph Staff Get 90 Minutes Notice Before Bein...
articles.full_text:
The new owners of the Daily Telegraph have made large numbers of staff redundant, telling them the title will be transformed from a newspaper “into a global, AI-powered premium media and intelligence business”.
In an all-company briefing and email on Friday morning, staff were told the title would rely increasingly on technology, data and AI to “reinvent the reader experience”. Newsroom insiders said they expected as many as 100 people to lose their jobs.
The “next chapter” of the Telegraph will focus on new revenue streams including “video, audio, puzzles, events, B2B, licensing, commerce and new products”, the CEO, Carolin Hulshoff Pol , wrote.
It will also focus on growing its audience internationally, “particularly in foreign affairs, defence and business”, she said.
Some staff were told on Thursday they were being fired, while others received calls and emails on Friday morning. Some senior staff were said to be in tears as they told colleagues their fate.
The culture and sports departments have been particularly hard hit, according to insiders. A source from inside the Telegraph said the atmosphere in the newsroom was “like a morgue”.
The Telegraph was bought in June by the European media group Axel Springer for £575m, ending three tortuous years for the title and its staff, during which potential owners were blocked, fell through or faced fierce internal opposition.
The paper joined a stable of media brands including the German titles Bild and Die Welt, as well as the digital outlets Politico and Business Insider. Mathias Döpfner, Axel Springer’s chief executive and controlling shareholder, said he intended to invest in the Telegraph to make it the “leading centre-right media outlet in the English-speaking world”.
However, heavy job cuts have been expected at the paper amid an internal staff consultation in recent weeks into the future of the business.
Pol said that during the lengthy sale process, “the Telegraph had limited ability to invest, adapt and move at the pace the market demanded”, adding that “the media world and technology have changed at extraordinary speed”.
“Our ambition is to transform the Telegraph from a leading British newspaper into a global, AI-powered premium media and intelligence business – built on trusted journalism, direct relationships with our audiences and expertise that sets us apart.
“To deliver on this ambition, we need to change how we are organised, how decisions are made, where we focus our resources and create efficiencies. We need clearer accountability, faster decision-making and a simpler, more effective organisation.”
She said the organisation would “use AI confidently while enhancing what technology cannot replace: judgment, originality, courage and trust”.
A spokesperson for the Telegraph Media Group reiterated Pol’s remarks, adding: “Today marks the start of a formal consultation process. These are difficult choices that we believe are necessary for the future of the business.”
TMG would not confirm the number of redundancies.

China, Europe should coordinate on carbon pricing, border tax: energy transition expert
Adair Turner urges Beijing and Brussels to unite on emission fees as the US pulls back from climate commitments
China and Europe should jointly introduce a system like the Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM), a levy on carbon-intensive imports designed to account for the carbon costs domestic producers face, which “applies against the rest of the world,” the co-chair of a global energy transition organisation says.
“The biggest single thing which I would love China to do is to say, ‘We want to join with Europe in a climate club’,” said Adair Turner, co-chair of the Energy Transitions Commission, during a panel discussion at the Bund Summit in Shanghai on Thursday.
Turner, who is also the former chairman of the UK’s Financial Services Authority, called on the two economies to commit jointly to carbon prices high enough to drive the decarbonisation of heavy industries such as cement and steel.
Calls for closer China-Europe climate cooperation have grown louder as the US retreats from international climate efforts under the Donald Trump administration, including its withdrawal from the Paris Agreement.

articles.title: Denmark to ban mink farming in government U-turn - BBC
articles.summary: Denmark to ban mink farming in government U-turn  BBCMajor victory: Denmark to end mink farming  Eurogroup for AnimalsDenmark pulls the plug on mink farming  Humane World for AnimalsVictory! Denmark Is Phasing Out Mink Fur Farming  PETA UKDenmark to end mink farming by August 2029 under EU ban  The Copenhagen Post
articles.full_text:
Mink farming will end in Denmark by August 2029 after the government decided to drop plans to pursue an exemption to an EU-wide ban on the practice.
Denmark was once the largest producer of mink fur in the world, but the industry has declined due to global bans on fur farming, a decline in the fur trade and an earlier outbreak of a Covid strain in the nation's mink population.
The ban is due to come into effect on 7 August next year, and is followed by a two-year transition period to phase out the practice.
Danish Nature Minister Christian Rabjerg Madsen said the government had chosen animal welfare.
"A business should not continue just because it has existed for a long time. It should also make sense for society, for the economy and for the animals," he said.
The Danish government had initially sought an exemption for its mink industry when the EU added the mammal to its list of invasive species in 2025, prohibiting people from keeping them.
However, the current coalition government, elected in June, reversed this decision and decided not to proceed with the application on Friday.
Social Democrat MP Brigitte Vind said it was "a good day for animal welfare".
"It is absolutely the right decision not to apply for a special scheme for mink breeding in Denmark," she said.
The Danish Mink Association, which represents breeders, has been approached for comment.
Denmark is one of the few European countries to still produce mink fur, one of the more common pelts used in making fur garments.
However, its production has slipped behind that of other countries, such as Poland and China, in recent years.
The industry faced a crisis during the coronavirus pandemic, when the government ordered a mass cull of mink after a mutated strain of Covid-19 was found in the animals. Approximately 15 million were killed.
At the time, the country had huge export markets to China and Hong Kong. The government later admitted it had no legal basis for the culling.
There are now approximately 15,000 mink left in Denmark.
No costs have yet been determined for closing Denmark's seven remaining mink farms, but an animal welfare spokesperson for one of the governing coalition parties previously estimated it would be around 14m Danish krone (£1.56m), local media report, but the final amount could be higher.
The wearing of fur is a controversial subject within fashion circles, with publications and fashion brands choosing not to use or promote it several years ago.
But it re-entered the spotlight last year, with celebrities and fashionistas wearing both vintage and so-called faux fur.

Businesses are in line for around £800 million in savings on paperwork under plans announced by the Chancellor, who wants to cut back on “form-filling and pointless paperwork”.
The measures, designed to give businesses “breathing space”, have been unveiled ahead of John Healey’s first Budget next week.
Mr Healey has said that he wants the Budget to ease cost pressures on both companies and households.
The Treasury expects streamlined reporting requirements to save £290 million.
Easing “duplicative reporting burdens” for asset managers is expected to save £105 million.
A further £116 million in savings is expected for businesses in the transaction chain from cutting red tape involved in buying and selling homes.
Import tariffs that were paused across sectors including chemicals, plastics, automotive and food and beverages had been due to expire at the end of December.
Instead, the suspensions are being extended for another year, covering more than 250 products.
According to the Treasury, that extension is due to save up to £155 million.
The measures form part of efforts to cut back the regulatory admin businesses are required to do by 25 per cent by the end of this Parliament.
Any remaining cost-saving measures will be set out in the Budget.
Mr Healey and Prime Minister Andy Burnham are due to meet small business leaders at No 10 North on Friday.
Mr Burnham said: “If you run a business, you want to spend your time serving your customers, creating jobs and growing your firm, not filling in unnecessary forms.
“It’s not right that pointless bureaucracy gets in the way of people working hard to build something that matters to their high street.
“So we’re getting government off their backs and giving businesses the breathing space to grow.
“Because when businesses succeed, they create good jobs, strengthen their communities and bring growth to every part of the country.”
Mr Healey said: “British firms are fed up with form-filling and pointless paperwork that eats into valuable time and money when they simply want to get on with running their businesses.
“That is why we are cutting unnecessary bureaucracy and giving businesses the breathing space they need to invest, innovate and create good jobs.”
The plans come against a tight fiscal backdrop, with UK government borrowing rising by more than expected to £24.5 billion for last month.
That undershoot of expectations underscores the constraints in the public finances ahead of the Chancellor’s Budget.
Higher borrowing costs are weighing down on fiscal headroom, and Mr Healey is expected to increase bank taxes in response.
He has rejected calls to hike capital gains tax at the Budget, amid concerns it could hamper economic growth.
